lessons.unit: Unit 1: Weather hazards (AQA 3.1.1 The challenge of natural hazards)
lessons.title: Global atmospheric circulation
objectives: Identify the Hadley, Ferrel and Polar cells on a circulation diagram
Explain where air rises and sinks and why this creates high and low pressure
Link pressure belts to wet and dry climates around the world

keywords.def: the large-scale movement of air around the Earth that moves heat from the Equator towards the poles
the circulation cell between the Equator and about 30 degrees north and south
the middle cell, between about 30 and 60 degrees north and south
the cell between about 60 degrees and the poles
an area where air is rising, often bringing cloud and rain
an area where air is sinking, often bringing dry, clear weather

starter: Say Bismillah. Define weather and define climate.
Name two places on Earth that are very hot. Which one is wet and which is dry?
What happens to warm air: does it rise or sink?

teach.heading: Why does the Earth need circulation?
bullets: The Sun heats the Equator most strongly because rays are concentrated there.
The poles receive less heat because rays are spread over a larger area.
Air movement carries heat from the Equator towards the poles.
teach.note: Misconception to correct: the Equator is not hot because it is closer to the Sun. The difference in distance is tiny. The same amount of energy is concentrated on a small area at the Equator but spread over a large, curved area near the poles. Use a torch on a globe or a ball held at different angles. Ask: if heat only stayed where it landed, what would the Equator and poles be like?

teach.heading: The three cells
bullets: Hadley cell: Equator to 30 degrees north and south.
Ferrel cell: 30 to 60 degrees north and south.
Polar cell: 60 degrees to the poles.
teach.note: Draw the diagram live and build it one cell at a time. Pupils must be able to reproduce and label it in an exam. Make the point that the three cells are connected like gears: the Hadley and Polar cells are driven by heating and cooling, and the Ferrel cell is driven by the other two. Check pupils can say north AND south because the pattern is mirrored.

teach.heading: Rising air and low pressure
bullets: At the Equator, hot air rises and leaves low pressure at the surface.
Rising air cools, water vapour condenses, clouds form and heavy rain falls.
At about 60 degrees, warm and cold air meet and rise again.
teach.note: Chain of reasoning for the 4-6 mark questions: heating, air rises, pressure at the surface falls, air cools as it rises, condensation, cloud, rainfall. Link to tropical rainforests (Amazon, Congo, Indonesia). Link 60 degrees north to the UK: unsettled, wet weather because the UK sits near this rising air. Misconception: low pressure does not mean cold; it means rising air.

teach.heading: Sinking air and high pressure
bullets: At about 30 degrees, cool air sinks, creating high pressure.
Sinking air warms and holds moisture, so skies are clear and dry.
At the poles, cold air sinks, giving cold, dry conditions.
teach.note: This is where the great hot deserts are found: Sahara, Arabian, Thar, Kalahari and Australian deserts are all close to 30 degrees north or south. Ask pupils to find these on a world map. Key correction: not every place at 30 degrees is a desert, because local factors such as mountains and ocean currents also affect climate. Link forward to lessons 5 to 8 on hot deserts.

teach.heading: Surface winds
bullets: Air moves at the surface from high pressure to low pressure.
Trade winds blow towards the Equator; westerlies blow towards 60 degrees.
The Earth's rotation bends winds, so they are not straight north or south.
teach.note: Keep this light for the first lesson: pupils need to know that wind is air moving from high to low pressure, and that the UK's prevailing wind is the south-westerly, bringing moist air from the Atlantic. The bending of winds (Coriolis effect) will return in lesson 2 for tropical storms. Ask: why are the UK's winters mild and wet compared with the same latitude in Canada?

practice: On a blank diagram, label the Equator, 30 degrees, 60 degrees and the poles, then mark where air rises (R) and sinks (S).
Complete the sentence: At 30 degrees north, air _____ so pressure is _____ and the weather is usually _____.
independent: Explain why tropical rainforests are found close to the Equator. Use the words rising, cooling, condensation and low pressure. (4 marks)
Explain why many hot deserts are found near 30 degrees north and south of the Equator. (4 marks)
Stretch: Explain why the UK has more unsettled weather than the Sahara. (6 marks)
exit: At which latitude does air rise to create low pressure, 0, 30 or 90 degrees?
In one sentence, explain why high pressure usually brings dry weather.
lessons.homework: Redraw the three-cell diagram from memory, label it, and write three sentences linking it to rainforests and deserts.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-labelled diagram with cut-out arrows to place. EAL: sentence frames 'Air rises at ... so ...'. Stretch: explain why the cells do not meet exactly at 30 and 60 degrees every day of the year.

lessons.title: Tropical cyclones: distribution, measurement and causes (3.1)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do tropical cyclones never form on the Equator?
objectives: To understand where tropical cyclones form, how they are measured and what causes them
successCriteria: All: describe the global distribution of tropical cyclones
Most: explain the conditions needed for a cyclone to form
Some: explain why none form within about 5° of the Equator
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: pressure, condensation and latent heat
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: humility before the power of nature

keywords.def: a large, rotating storm with very low pressure and strong winds, forming over warm oceans
the effect of the Earth's spin that makes moving air turn
a change in wind speed or direction with height
a 1 to 5 scale of cyclone strength based on wind speed
the calm, clear centre of a cyclone

hook.text: A storm is called a hurricane in Florida, a typhoon in Japan and a cyclone in Bangladesh. Is it the same thing?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'It is He who shows you lightning, causing fear and hope, and brings up the heavy clouds' (ar-Ra'd 13:12). The Prophet, peace be upon him, when he saw strong wind, would ask Allah for its good and seek refuge from its harm (Sahih Muslim). Muslims prepare wisely and turn to Allah in every storm.

starter.q: Name an ocean where hurricanes form.

teach.heading: Where they form
bullets: Between about 5° and 30° north and south
Most in late summer and autumn
teach.note: Names by region: hurricanes (Atlantic, north-east Pacific), typhoons (north-west Pacific), cyclones (Indian Ocean, South Pacific).

teach.heading: Conditions needed
teach.note: Warm water must be deep (tens of metres) to keep feeding the storm.

teach.heading: How a cyclone builds
bullets: More air rushes in and spins
teach.note: It weakens over land or cooler water: its energy source is cut off.
cycle: Air drawn in and spun by Coriolis
Storm grows while over warm sea

teach.heading: Measuring cyclones
bullets: Category 5: winds of at least 252 km/h
teach.note: Also measured: central pressure, rainfall and storm surge height; satellites track them.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Why do cyclones not form within about 5° of the Equator?
options: The Coriolis force is too weak to make them spin
check.why: The sea is warm enough, but the Coriolis force is almost zero near the Equator.

practice.q: Describe the global distribution of tropical cyclones. (3 marks)
practice.a: Between about 5° and 30° N and S (1); over warm oceans such as the Caribbean, north-west Pacific, Bay of Bengal (1); none on the Equator or in the South Atlantic in most years (1)
practice.model:
Describe = pattern plus examples plus anomaly.
Pattern: in the tropics, 5° to 30° N and S.
Examples: Caribbean, north-west Pacific, Bay of Bengal.
Anomaly: almost none on the Equator.

practice.q: State the minimum sea temperature usually needed. (1 mark)
practice.a: About 26.5 °C (accept 26 to 27 °C)

practice.q: Explain why a cyclone weakens over land. (2 marks)
practice.a: It loses its supply of warm, moist air (1), so less condensation and heat to power it (1); friction also slows it

independent.q: Core: 'Explain the causes of tropical cyclones.' (6 marks) Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Warm sea above about 26.5 °C heats moist air which rises, creating low pressure; condensation releases latent heat, strengthening the updraught; Coriolis force (beyond 5°) makes the air spiral; low wind shear lets the structure grow; explained links between factors
independent.model: Teacher plans it first: 1) warm sea and rising moist air; 2) condensation releases heat, so more air is drawn in; 3) Coriolis spins it; 4) low wind shear lets it grow tall. Link each with 'which means' or 'so'.

independent.q: Extend: Suggest why the number of strong cyclones might change as oceans warm. (3 marks)
independent.a: Warmer seas cover a larger area and supply more energy (1), so more intense storms are possible (1); some areas may see more, others fewer (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Compare the Saffir-Simpson scale with measuring rainfall as a way to show a cyclone's danger. (2 marks)
independent.a: Saffir-Simpson only measures wind (1); much damage comes from flooding and storm surge, so rainfall and surge matter too (1)

exit.q: A typhoon forms in the:
exit.a: North-west Pacific

exit.q: Big question: why do tropical cyclones never form on the Equator?
exit.a: The Coriolis force is too weak there to make the storm spin

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Weather hazards (AQA 3.1.1 The challenge of natural hazards)
lessons.title: Typhoon Haiyan: structure and effects
objectives: Describe the structure of a tropical storm including the eye and eye wall
Describe the primary and secondary effects of Typhoon Haiyan (2013)
Outline immediate and long-term responses and compare them

keywords.def: the calm centre of a tropical storm where air sinks and skies are often clear
the ring of towering clouds around the eye with the strongest winds and heaviest rain
the direct, immediate damage caused by a hazard
knock-on problems that follow, such as disease or loss of jobs
actions taken in the hours and days after a disaster, such as rescue and emergency aid
actions taken in the following months and years, such as rebuilding

starter: Say Bismillah. State two conditions needed for a tropical storm to form.
What is the name for a tropical storm in the north-west Pacific?
Define primary effects and secondary effects of a natural hazard.

teach.heading: Structure of a tropical storm
bullets: The eye is 30 to 50 km wide: sinking air, light winds, few clouds.
The eye wall has the strongest winds and torrential rain.
Cloud bands spiral outward; the whole storm can be hundreds of kilometres wide.
teach.note: Draw a cross-section. Emphasise that air sinks in the eye, which is why it is calm and often clear, but rises rapidly in the eye wall. A frequent misconception is that the eye is the most dangerous part; the eye wall is. People who think the storm has passed when the eye arrives can be caught out by the second half. Wind speed must reach about 119 km/h to be classed as a hurricane or typhoon.

teach.heading: Case study: Typhoon Haiyan, 2013
bullets: Struck the Philippines on 8 November 2013 with winds over 300 km/h.
Philippines is a newly emerging economy (NEE) with many people on the coast.
Storm surge in Tacloban reached several metres, flooding coastal areas.
teach.note: Locate the Philippines on a map, between the Pacific and the South China Sea; lots of islands, many low-lying coastal communities and poor-quality housing. The typhoon made landfall in the central Philippines (Leyte and Samar). Wind speeds were among the strongest ever recorded at landfall. Keep figures approximate: over 6,000 deaths, about four million displaced, over one million homes damaged. Stress the human side with compassion.

teach.heading: Primary and secondary effects
bullets: Primary: over 6,000 people died; over 1 million homes damaged or destroyed.
Primary: roads, airports and power lines were destroyed.
Secondary: food and clean water shortages, disease, and loss of livelihoods.
teach.note: Ask pupils to classify further effects as primary or secondary: crops destroyed (primary, farmers' livelihoods lost then secondary), looting (secondary), people homeless (primary/secondary depending on explanation). Include environmental effects: coconut plantations and mangroves destroyed. Make sure pupils use figures from the case study; examiners reward place-specific detail.

teach.heading: Immediate and long-term responses
bullets: Immediate: international aid, rescue, food, water and temporary shelter.
Immediate: damaged roads and airports slowed the delivery of aid.
Long-term: rebuilding homes, replanting mangroves, better shelters and warning.
teach.note: Many countries and charities sent aid, including Muslim charities. Ask pupils: why was getting aid to remote islands so hard? Long-term: 'build back better' by constructing stronger homes further from the coast, reinforcing storm shelters, and restoring mangroves that act as natural barriers. Compare an NEE with a wealthy country: more reliance on overseas aid. Do not overstate; keep to widely reported actions.

practice: Label a diagram of a tropical storm: eye, eye wall, rising air, sinking air, spiralling cloud.
Complete a table with columns Primary / Secondary / Immediate / Long-term for Typhoon Haiyan using three facts each.
independent: Describe the structure of a tropical storm. (3 marks)
Using a named tropical storm, explain its primary and secondary effects. (6 marks)
Stretch: Assess the importance of immediate responses compared with long-term responses after Haiyan. (6 marks)
exit: Which part of a tropical storm has the strongest winds: the eye or the eye wall?
Give one secondary effect of Typhoon Haiyan.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word news report on Haiyan using at least four facts and one human impact.
lessons.send: SEND: case study fact-sheet with highlighted facts. EAL: key words with pictures. Stretch: compare Haiyan with a tropical storm that hit a high-income country.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Weather hazards (AQA 3.1.1 The challenge of natural hazards)
lessons.title: Reducing the effects of tropical storms
objectives: Describe how monitoring, prediction, protection and planning reduce risk
Explain how each strategy saves lives or reduces damage
Evaluate which strategies are most effective in a country such as the Philippines

keywords.def: tracking a hazard using tools such as satellites, radar and weather stations
forecasting where and when a hazard will strike and how strong it will be
actions that reduce damage, such as strong buildings and sea defences
preparing people and land use before a hazard, including evacuation routes and drills
a coastal tree that grows in salt water and reduces wave and surge energy

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the two parts of a tropical storm's structure and what each is like.
Give one primary effect and one secondary effect of Typhoon Haiyan.
What is meant by an immediate response?

teach.heading: Four ways to manage risk
bullets: Monitoring: satellites, aircraft and radar track storms.
Prediction: forecasts give the path, strength and landfall time.
Protection: buildings and defences resist wind, flood and surge.
Planning: evacuation routes, drills, education and land-use zoning.
teach.note: Introduce the acronym MPPP or the four words in order. Ask pupils which is cheapest (planning, education) and which is expensive (sea walls, strong buildings). Note: these are the same four ideas used for tectonic hazards, so pupils can transfer knowledge. Ask pupils which strategies need money and technology and which can work in a poorer country.

teach.heading: Monitoring and prediction
bullets: Satellites show storm position and size; planes fly into the storm for data.
Forecasts are issued days ahead so people can leave.
Predictions have limits: the exact path and strength can still change.
teach.note: Explain the 'cone of uncertainty' on a forecast map. Accuracy has improved because of satellites and supercomputers. Limitation: forecasting rapid strengthening is harder. A good evaluation point: warnings only save lives if people receive them, understand them, and have somewhere safe to go. Mention text alerts and local radio.

teach.heading: Protection and planning
bullets: Strong buildings: reinforced roofs and stilts keep homes above floods.
Cyclone shelters and sea walls protect people on the coast.
Mangroves and drills reduce damage and speed up evacuation.
teach.note: Compare cost: mangrove restoration is low cost and environmentally friendly; sea walls are expensive. Land-use planning means keeping essential buildings away from the shore. In a poorer country, community training and low-cost techniques are more realistic. Link to the Philippines after Haiyan: shelters, early warning, relocation inland, mangrove replanting.

teach.heading: Which strategy is best?
bullets: Prediction saves lives only if people can act on warnings.
Protection reduces damage but is costly for poorer countries.
A combination of strategies is usually most effective.
teach.note: Model an evaluative paragraph: Point (monitoring is effective), Evidence (e.g. forecasts allowed evacuations), Explanation, then a counter-point and judgement. Teach pupils to finish with a clear, justified decision, not 'it depends'. This builds the 6-mark skills needed for AQA.

practice: Match each strategy to its example: monitoring, prediction, protection, planning, with the examples satellites, forecasts, sea walls, evacuation drills.
Write a Point-Evidence-Explain paragraph on why forecasts save lives.
independent: Explain how planning and preparation can reduce the effects of a tropical storm. (4 marks)
'Protection is the most effective way to reduce the impact of tropical storms.' To what extent do you agree? (6 marks)
Stretch: Design a low-cost storm-safety plan for a coastal village in the Philippines and justify three choices.
exit: Define monitoring.
Give one reason why a poorer country may struggle to build sea walls.
lessons.homework: Create a one-page storm preparation leaflet for a family living on a coast, using the four strategies.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters for the 6-mark evaluation. EAL: bilingual glossary. Stretch: research how Bangladesh cyclone shelters reduced deaths.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Hot desert environments (AQA 3.1.2 The living world)
lessons.title: Hot deserts: climate, location and adaptations
objectives: Locate the world's main hot deserts and describe their climate
Explain why hot deserts occur at about 30 degrees north and south
Describe how plants and animals adapt to desert conditions

keywords.def: a dry area with less than 250 mm of rain a year and very high daytime temperatures
the difference between the highest daytime and lowest night-time temperature
a feature that helps a plant or animal survive in its environment
active at night rather than during the day
a plant adapted to survive in very dry conditions

starter: Say Bismillah. At what latitude does air sink to create high pressure?
Why does sinking air bring dry weather?
Name two hot deserts you know.

teach.heading: Where are hot deserts?
bullets: Found around 15 to 30 degrees north and south of the Equator.
Examples: Sahara, Arabian, Thar, Kalahari, Great Victoria.
Many are in the centre or west of continents.
teach.note: Use a world map with the Tropics marked. Pupils should link directly to lesson 1: sinking air at about 30 degrees means high pressure and clear skies. Add the local factors: distance from the sea, rain-shadow effects and cold ocean currents, such as in the Namib. The Arabian Peninsula is relevant for pupils' own knowledge; the Rub' al-Khali is one of the largest sand deserts in the world.

teach.heading: Desert climate
bullets: Very low rainfall: under 250 mm a year, and unreliable.
Daytime temperatures often above 40 degrees Celsius.
Clear skies cause big falls at night, so the diurnal range is large.
teach.note: Use a climate graph of a hot desert (e.g. Cairo or a Sahara site). Pupils practise describing a climate graph: state rainfall total, highest and lowest temperatures, and use units. Explain the large diurnal range: no cloud, so heat escapes quickly at night, and the dry air holds little heat. Misconception: deserts are not always sand; many are rocky or stony.

teach.heading: Plant adaptations
bullets: Cacti store water in thick stems.
Spines instead of leaves reduce water loss.
Long or wide roots reach water deep down or after rainfall.
teach.note: Ask for 'feature then function' explanations: the waxy skin reduces water loss because it limits evaporation. Introduce the word adaptation as a feature that helps survival. Some seeds lie dormant for years until rain comes, then bloom quickly. Pupils should give two or three adaptations with a reason for each, as in an exam.

teach.heading: Animal adaptations
bullets: Camel: stores fat in its hump and has wide feet for sand.
Fennec fox: large ears lose heat; pale fur reflects the Sun.
Many animals are nocturnal or burrow to avoid the heat.
teach.note: Camels do not store water in their humps; they store fat. This is a very common misconception. Camels can also tolerate large changes in body temperature and drink large amounts quickly. The kangaroo rat gets water from seeds. Link Arabian camel and Bedouin knowledge for context and note that Allah has equipped creation for each environment; a good moment for reflection without pressing doctrine.

practice: Describe the location of the Sahara Desert using the latitude lines on the map. (2 marks)
Complete a table: adaptation, plant or animal, and how it helps survival, for cactus, camel and fennec fox.
independent: Explain why hot deserts are found around 30 degrees north and south. (4 marks)
Describe the climate shown on the climate graph for a hot desert. (3 marks)
Stretch: Explain how the structure of a cactus reflects the climate it lives in. (4 marks)
exit: State the maximum annual rainfall of a hot desert.
Explain one way a camel is adapted to the desert.
lessons.homework: Draw and annotate one desert plant and one desert animal showing at least three adaptations.
lessons.send: SEND: adaptation matching cards. EAL: picture glossary. Stretch: explain why the Atacama is so dry despite not being at 30 degrees in the same way as the Sahara.

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Hot desert environments (AQA 3.1.2 The living world)
lessons.title: Hot desert opportunities and challenges: the Thar Desert
objectives: Locate the Thar Desert and describe its main features
Describe opportunities for development in the Thar Desert
Explain the challenges of extreme temperatures and water supply

keywords.def: a chance to develop economically, such as through mining or farming
a difficulty that limits development, such as extreme heat or lack of water
supplying water to land using canals, pipes or sprinklers to grow crops
underground rock that stores water
how easy it is to reach and travel around a place
a small earth-dam that traps rainwater, used in Rajasthan

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two ways plants or animals adapt to desert conditions.
What is the rainfall total that defines a hot desert?
Name a desert in Asia.

teach.heading: Where is the Thar Desert?
bullets: In north-west India (mainly Rajasthan) and eastern Pakistan.
India's Thar is one of the world's most heavily populated deserts.
Hot summers; low, unreliable rainfall; sand dunes and rocky plains.
teach.note: Locate it on a map with the Indus plain and the Aravalli hills. Ask pupils why more people live here than in the Sahara. Describe climate: summer temperatures often above 45 degrees Celsius; a monsoon influence brings some rain between July and September but it is unreliable. Key point: the Thar is the case study for AQA hot desert development in this course.

teach.heading: Opportunities for development
bullets: Mining: minerals such as gypsum, limestone and sandstone.
Energy: large solar farms in the strong, reliable sunshine.
Tourism: camel safaris and historic cities like Jaisalmer.
teach.note: Link each opportunity to a physical feature of the desert: solar farms use clear skies and flat land; tourism uses unique landscape and culture; farming uses irrigation. Mention the Indira Gandhi Canal, which brings water from the Himalayan rivers over hundreds of kilometres and has allowed crops such as wheat and cotton to be grown. Ask pupils which opportunity creates most jobs.

teach.heading: Challenge: extreme temperatures
bullets: Heat above 45 degrees Celsius makes outdoor work dangerous.
Evaporation is high, so water is lost quickly from soil and reservoirs.
Heat limits farming and tourism in summer.
teach.note: Ask pupils to think of workers and tourists: heat stroke risk, extra cost of cooling buildings, crops wilting. Ask: how does heat make the water challenge worse? Pupils should make a link between evaporation and water supply. A strong answer connects temperature to its human impact.

teach.heading: Challenge: water supply and accessibility
bullets: Rain is low and unreliable; groundwater in aquifers is being used up.
Johads and canals help, but supplies are limited.
Remote areas have poor roads, so building and tourism are harder.
teach.note: Sources of water: rainfall collected in johads, canals such as the Indira Gandhi Canal, and wells that reach aquifers. Falling water tables mean wells have to go deeper. Accessibility: loose sand and long distances make roads and pipelines expensive. Make sure pupils see that each opportunity is limited by a challenge.

teach.heading: Balancing the two
bullets: Population growth increases demand for water and food.
Climate change may make rainfall less predictable.
Development must be sustainable to protect people and land.
teach.note: Ask: is it right to develop a fragile desert? Use the 'opportunity, challenge, judgement' approach. Link to stewardship: the Qur'an teaches that we are khalifah on Earth (2:30) and should not cause corruption on it after it has been set in order (7:56). This leads naturally into lessons 7 and 8 on desertification.

practice: Complete an opportunity/challenge table for the Thar using at least three of each.
Explain how the Indira Gandhi Canal has helped farming in the Thar.
independent: Explain two opportunities for economic development in a hot desert. (4 marks)
Explain why extreme temperatures are a challenge for development in hot deserts. (3 marks)
Stretch: 'The opportunities of developing hot deserts outweigh the challenges.' Discuss using the Thar. (6 marks)
exit: Name one mineral or resource that can be developed in the Thar.
Give one reason why water supply is a challenge in the Thar.
lessons.homework: Write a 6-mark answer to: 'Explain the challenges of developing a hot desert environment.'
lessons.send: SEND: model answer with missing words and a fact bank. EAL: sentence starters. Stretch: compare the Thar with another hot desert such as the Sahara.

lessons.title: Fragile environments: causes of desertification and deforestation (7.1)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why are some environments so easily damaged?
objectives: To understand where fragile environments are and the causes of desertification and deforestation
successCriteria: All: name four fragile environments and locate them
Most: explain four causes of desertification
Some: explain the causes of deforestation and how they link
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: ecosystems and biodiversity

keywords.def: an environment that is easily damaged and slow to recover
land turning into desert, usually at the edge of existing deserts
the large-scale removal of forest
too many animals eating the vegetation
the semi-arid strip south of the Sahara

hook.text: If a forest takes 100 years to grow and one day to cut down, how should we decide whether to cut it?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Do not cause corruption on the earth after it has been set right' (al-A'raf 7:56), and made people successors on the earth (al-An'am 6:165). Caring for fragile environments is part of this trust (amanah).

starter.q: A tropical cyclone needs sea of at least about:

starter.a: For example: hot desert, tropical rainforest, polar, mountain, coral reef

teach.heading: Fragile environments
teach.note: Fragile: easily damaged, slow to recover, finely balanced ecosystems.

teach.heading: Causes of desertification
teach.note: The Sahel is the classic example: semi-arid land between the Sahara and the savanna.

teach.heading: Causes of deforestation
teach.note: In the Amazon, cattle ranching is the largest single cause.

teach.heading: Linking causes
teach.note: Model: explain a chain, not a list.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Which is a physical cause of desertification?
check.why: Drought is physical; the other two are human causes.

practice.q: Explain how population growth can cause desertification. (3 marks)
practice.a: More people need more food and fuel (1), so more grazing, cultivation and wood cutting (1), removing vegetation so soil is eroded by wind and rain (1)
practice.model:
Start with the cause: more people.
Add the action: more animals, crops and fuelwood.
Add the effect on land: vegetation removed, soil exposed and eroded.
That is a chain.

practice.q: Name the region south of the Sahara affected by desertification. (1 mark)
practice.a: The Sahel

practice.q: State two causes of deforestation in the Amazon. (2 marks)
practice.a: Two of: cattle ranching, soy farming, logging, mining, roads, dams

independent.q: Core: 'Explain the causes of desertification.' (6 marks) Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Physical: drought, rising temperatures; human: population growth, overgrazing, overcultivation, fuelwood; explained chains with a named area (the Sahel)
independent.model: Teacher plans it first: P1 drought (physical) and why it matters; P2 population and overgrazing chain; P3 fuelwood; link: human and physical causes reinforce each other.

independent.q: Extend: Suggest why poorer communities may have little choice but to damage fragile land. (3 marks)
independent.a: They depend on farming and wood for food and fuel (1); few alternatives or money (1); short-term survival comes before long-term care (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Compare the causes of desertification and deforestation. (2 marks)
independent.a: Both driven by population and farming pressure (1); desertification also by drought, deforestation more by commercial ranching and logging (1)

exit.q: Overgrazing is:
exit.a: Too many animals eating the vegetation
options: Too many animals eating the vegetation

exit.q: Big question: why are some environments so easily damaged?
exit.a: Their ecosystems are finely balanced and slow to recover, so human pressure and drought quickly degrade them

lessons.unit: Unit 2: Hot desert environments (AQA 3.1.2 The living world)
lessons.title: Reducing the risk of desertification
objectives: Describe water and soil management strategies for reducing desertification
Explain how each strategy works and why appropriate technology suits poorer areas
Evaluate and write a 6-mark answer on reducing desertification

keywords.def: simple, low-cost tools and methods that local people can make and maintain
the build-up of salt in soil, often caused by poor irrigation in hot climates
lines of stones laid along contours to slow runoff and trap water and soil
a salt-tolerant shrub planted to stabilise soil and provide fodder for animals
meeting present needs without harming the ability of future generations to meet theirs

starter: Say Bismillah. Define desertification.
Give two human causes of desertification.
Explain how soil erosion can make desertification worse.

teach.heading: Water management
bullets: Rainwater harvesting: johads and ponding banks trap rain.
Drip irrigation delivers water slowly to roots, reducing waste.
Poor irrigation causes salinisation, so efficient methods matter.
teach.note: Salinisation: in hot dry places water evaporates quickly and leaves salts behind, so heavily irrigated soil can become too salty for crops. Drip irrigation reduces evaporation and the amount of salt left in the soil. Pupils should know the connection between evaporation and salt build-up. The link to Rajasthan's johads recalls lesson 6.

teach.heading: Soil management
bullets: Stone bunds and contour traps slow runoff and trap soil.
Planting trees and shrubs such as Atriplex holds soil with roots.
Manure improves soil; crop rotation prevents over-cultivation.
teach.note: Explain that stone lines laid along the contours slow rainwater, which then soaks in rather than washing the soil away. They are cheap and can be built by villagers with local stones. Atriplex is salt-tolerant and gives animal feed. Trees also give shade and wind protection. Remind pupils of the Prophet's words recorded by al-Bukhari and Muslim: when a Muslim plants a tree or sows a crop and a person, bird or animal eats from it, it is charity (sadaqah) for him.

teach.heading: Appropriate technology
bullets: Low-cost, simple tools that local people can use and repair.
Villages use stones, manure and hand tools rather than machines.
Local ownership means projects continue after outside help ends.
teach.note: Compare with expensive solutions such as large dams and pipelines, which poorer countries may not afford or maintain. Appropriate technology is cheaper and local people are involved in the decisions. Ask pupils: why might a project fail if local people are not involved?

teach.heading: Evaluating strategies
bullets: Cheap local methods are sustainable and easy to maintain.
Large schemes need money, skills and may disturb local people.
Success depends on education, community involvement and funding.
teach.note: Model the 6-mark structure: (1) identify two strategies, (2) explain how each works, (3) compare cost and sustainability, (4) give a clear judgement. Use the plan from the Drive: a flow chart linking strategies to the problem they address, to the level of development, and the limits of each. Mark with the class and ask pupils to self-mark using the mark scheme levels.

practice: Make a flow chart linking each strategy (stone bunds, tree planting, rainwater harvesting, drip irrigation) to the cause of desertification it reduces.
Explain why Atriplex planting is useful on the edge of a desert.
independent: Explain how soil management can reduce the risk of desertification. (4 marks)
Explain why appropriate technology is suited to poorer countries. (3 marks)
Stretch: 'Water management is the most important way to reduce desertification.' How far do you agree? (6 marks)
exit: Define appropriate technology.
Explain how stone bunds help prevent soil erosion.
lessons.homework: Complete a 6-mark exam question on reducing the risk of desertification, using the PEE structure, and self-mark it.
lessons.send: SEND: model answer with key words missing; connect-the-words sheet. EAL: key word bank with pictures. Stretch: link strategies to named areas and levels of development.

lessons.title: What is a natural hazard, and why does risk vary?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why can the same hazard kill thousands in one place and almost nobody in another?
objectives: Define a natural hazard and classify hazards as tectonic, weather or other types
Explain why some hazards pose a greater risk to people than others
Explain how vulnerability, capacity to cope and the nature of the hazard affect risk
successCriteria: All: define hazard and give two examples of each main type
Most: explain at least two factors that increase risk
Some: use hazard, vulnerability and capacity to cope together to explain a contrast between two places
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: using a simple risk ratio to compare places
lessons.smsc: Moral: our duty of care (amanah) to protect vulnerable people; reflecting on the power of creation with humility

keywords.def: a natural event that threatens people or property
the probability that people will be harmed by a hazard
how likely people are to be harmed because of where and how they live
the ability of people to prepare for, survive and recover from a hazard
the size or strength of a hazard event

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two weather events that can be dangerous in the UK.
What is the difference between weather and climate?
Give one way that rainfall can become dangerous to people.

teach.heading: Types of natural hazard

head: Type
Examples
Main cause
rows: Slope, rock, weather and vegetation together

teach.note: Start by asking for examples before showing the table. Make the point that tectonic hazards come from inside the Earth and weather hazards from the atmosphere, but they can combine: an earthquake can trigger a tsunami or landslide; a storm can trigger a flood. AQA questions on 3.1.1.1 expect you to define a hazard and to state types, so insist on the exact definition: an event that threatens people or property. Stress that without people there is no hazard, only a natural event.

teach.heading: Hazard or disaster?

misconception.wrong: A natural hazard is the same thing as a natural disaster.
misconception.right: A hazard is the threat. It becomes a disaster when it meets vulnerable people and causes serious losses.

teach.note: Use two imagined villages: the same flood hits both, one has a warning system and raised homes. Which suffers a disaster? Pupils should see that disaster depends on people, not only the event. This is a common one-mark loss in definition questions. Link to amanah: we are asked to care for people and places, and reducing vulnerability is part of that care.

teach.heading: Factors that affect risk

right.title: People and place
points: Capacity to cope: money, planning, services
Living in risky areas such as flood plains

teach.note: Ask pupils to place each factor in the correct column on mini-whiteboards. Explain that hazards that strike suddenly with no warning (earthquakes) tend to be riskier than slow ones (drought), even at similar magnitude, because people cannot act in time. Stress that capacity to cope is mainly about money, governance and preparation. A simplified model is: risk rises with the size of the hazard and with vulnerability, and falls with capacity to cope. Present this as a teaching model, not a precise formula.

teach.heading: Model answer: explain why risk differs

model.problem: Two cities are each struck by a magnitude 7 earthquake. City A is in a low-income country with crowded, poorly built homes. City B is in a high-income country with strict building codes. Explain why risk is greater in City A. (4 marks)
steps: Point 1: homes in City A are poorly built, so they collapse and more people are trapped (vulnerability).
Point 2: City A has less money for emergency services, hospitals and rescue equipment (low capacity to cope).
Point 3: high population density means more people are close to the hazard.
Link each point to risk with a connective: 'which means', 'therefore', 'as a result'.
model.answer: Risk is greater in City A because its buildings are poorly built, so they are more likely to collapse and kill people, which makes people more vulnerable. City A also has less money for rescue teams and hospitals, so it has a lower capacity to cope and more people die as a result.

teach.note: I do. Show how each mark is a developed point: a fact then a reason. Underline the connectives in the model. Pupils often list factors without explaining how they change risk. The two cities are imagined: the case studies in the next lessons give real figures.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which change would most reduce the risk to a coastal community from storms?
options: A new early-warning system and storm shelters
More people building homes on the shore
check.why: B reduces vulnerability and increases capacity to cope. A, C and D each increase risk. Pupils choosing C may think the question is about location only.

teach.note: Answer: B. Ask a pupil who chose C to explain; use it to revisit that vulnerability grows when more people live in danger zones.

practice: Classify each hazard as tectonic, weather or flooding: volcanic eruption, drought, blizzard, tsunami, river flood, heatwave.
Complete the sentence stems: 'Vulnerability means...' and 'Capacity to cope means...'.
independent: Core: Define the term 'natural hazard'. (2 marks) Give two factors that can increase the risk from a hazard. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain why some hazards pose a greater risk to people than others. (4 marks)
Stretch: 'Poverty is the most important factor affecting the risk from natural hazards.' How far do you agree? (6 marks)
exit: Which of these is a hazard and which is a disaster: a river rising, or a river flooding 500 homes with deaths?
Return to the big question: give two reasons the same hazard can have different effects in two places.
lessons.homework: Find a news report of a hazard in the last five years. Make a table with the hazard, the place, and two factors that increased or reduced the risk. About 100 words.
lessons.send: SEND: sort-card activity for hazards types and a sentence frame for 'X means risk is higher because...'. EAL: picture glossary for hazard, risk, vulnerable. Stretch: compare how risk might change over time in one place as it urbanises.

lessons.title: Earthquakes and volcanoes: distribution, measurement and causes (3.1)
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do most earthquakes and volcanoes happen in narrow belts?
objectives: To understand the distribution, measurement and causes of earthquakes and volcanoes
successCriteria: All: describe where earthquakes and volcanoes occur
Most: explain what happens at each type of plate boundary
Some: explain how hotspots cause volcanoes away from plate boundaries
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: the structure of the Earth
lessons.smsc: Moral: our duty to help victims of disasters

keywords.def: where two tectonic plates meet
a plume of hot mantle that melts through the crust far from a boundary
one plate sinking beneath another
a scale measuring the energy released by an earthquake
a 1 to 12 scale of an earthquake's effects

hook.text: Iceland has volcanoes but Britain does not. What is different about where they are?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'When the earth is shaken with its final earthquake' (az-Zalzalah 99:1), and describes mountains as pegs (an-Naba' 78:7). Earthquakes remind Muslims of the Day of Judgement and of the duty to prepare, build safely and help those affected.

starter.q: A tropical cyclone needs sea of at least about:
The Earth's outer layer is the:
Which plate boundary type pulls apart?
Name the belt of volcanoes around the Pacific.

teach.heading: Distribution
bullets: A few at hotspots, like Hawaii
teach.note: Most of the world's active volcanoes and earthquakes are around the Pacific.

teach.heading: Plate boundaries
teach.note: Use examples.

teach.heading: Hotspots
teach.note: The Hawaiian islands get older to the north-west as the Pacific plate moves.

teach.heading: Measuring
bullets: Each whole number is about 32 times more energy
Mercalli: effects I to XII; volcanoes: VEI 0 to 8
teach.note: Seismometers record shaking. The Richter scale is older and now rarely used for large quakes.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Which boundary has earthquakes but no volcanoes?
check.why: At conservative boundaries plates slide past; no magma rises, so no volcanoes.

practice.q: Explain why volcanoes form at destructive boundaries. (3 marks)
practice.a: Oceanic plate subducts beneath continental (1); it melts in the mantle, forming magma (1); magma rises through cracks and erupts explosively (1)
practice.model:
Chain of reasoning:
Oceanic plate is denser, so it sinks (subducts).
It melts as it goes down into the hot mantle.
The magma rises and erupts: a volcano.

practice.q: How much more energy is released by a magnitude 7 than a magnitude 6? (1 mark)
practice.a: About 32 times

practice.q: State one difference between magnitude and intensity. (2 marks)
practice.a: Magnitude measures energy released at the source (1); intensity measures effects at a place, which vary with distance (1)

independent.q: Core: 'Explain the global distribution of earthquakes and volcanoes.' (6 marks) Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Most lie along plate boundaries, especially the Ring of Fire; explained by subduction at destructive boundaries, rising magma at constructive, friction at conservative; hotspots explain exceptions like Hawaii
independent.model: Teacher plans it first: P1 pattern (belts, Ring of Fire) with explanation; P2 destructive boundaries; P3 constructive and conservative; P4 hotspot anomaly.

independent.q: Extend: Suggest why Iceland has both volcanoes and earthquakes. (3 marks)
independent.a: It lies on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, a constructive boundary (1), where plates pull apart and magma rises (1); there is also a hotspot beneath it (1)

independent.q: Stretch: Why is the Mercalli scale useful to planners? (2 marks)
independent.a: It shows effects on buildings and people in each place (1), so planners know where damage is worst (1)

exit.q: Hawaii's volcanoes are caused by a:
exit.a: Hotspot

exit.q: Big question: why do most earthquakes and volcanoes happen in narrow belts?
exit.a: They are along plate boundaries where plates move apart, together or past each other

lessons.title: Tectonic hazards: effects, responses, and reducing the risk
lessons.bigQuestion: If tectonic hazards are so dangerous, why do millions of people live with them?
objectives: Distinguish primary from secondary effects and immediate from long-term responses
Explain why people continue to live in tectonically active areas
Evaluate monitoring, prediction, protection and planning as ways to reduce risk
successCriteria: All: sort effects into primary and secondary and responses into immediate and long-term
Most: give three reasons people live near tectonic hazards
Some: judge which risk-reduction strategy is most effective, with reasons
lessons.crossCurricular: Technology: seismometers and building engineering
lessons.smsc: Moral: compassion and help for those affected; fairness in sharing resources between rich and poor countries

keywords.def: damage caused directly by the hazard itself
damage that follows later because of the primary effects
action in the hours and days after a hazard
action in the months and years that follow
forecasting when and where a hazard will happen
measuring changes that might warn of a hazard

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the three main types of plate margin.
State what happens at a conservative margin.
Explain what 'subduction' means.

teach.heading: Effects and responses

head: Timing
Effects
Responses
rows: Buildings collapse; people killed or injured; roads and power cut
Search and rescue; first aid; emergency shelters; food, water and medicine
Fires, landslides, tsunami; disease; unemployment; homelessness
Rebuilding; new building codes; money from insurance or aid; restoring jobs

teach.note: Be exact with the terms. Primary effects happen as a direct result of the ground shaking or the eruption. Secondary effects are knock-on, for example fires from broken gas pipes or disease from damaged water supplies. Immediate responses are in the first hours and days; long-term responses take months or years. The table headers deliberately pair the two vocabularies so pupils can see both. Ask for examples of each from their own knowledge. Case-study detail follows next lesson.

teach.heading: Why do people stay?
bullets: Geothermal energy, minerals and tourism provide jobs.
Family ties, culture and no money to move.
Hazard is rare, or people believe it will not happen to them.
teach.note: Ask: would you leave your home? Pupils usually say yes, then realise how much money, family and work are tied to a place. In Iceland, geothermal power heats most homes. Around Mount Vesuvius and Mount Etna, soils are fertile. Many people are not aware of the danger or have no choice. Be sensitive: some pupils may have family in earthquake zones; keep the tone respectful and factual.

teach.heading: Four ways to reduce risk

left.title: Before: monitor and predict
points: Gas and ground tilt measured on volcanoes

right.title: Before: protect and plan
points: Earthquake-proof buildings: cross-bracing, shock absorbers, deep foundations
Land-use zoning away from risk areas

teach.note: Explain that monitoring uses instruments, prediction is the forecast, protection is the physical design, and planning is the organisation (evacuation routes, zoning, drills). Ask: why can volcanoes sometimes be predicted but earthquakes not? Volcanoes give measurable warning signs such as rising gas and small tremors; the build-up to earthquakes is not reliably measurable. Wealthy places can afford more of all four, which links back to capacity to cope.

teach.heading: Skill: evaluate a strategy

model.problem: 'Earthquake-proof building is the best way to reduce the risk from earthquakes.' How far do you agree? (4 marks)
steps: Start with an argument for: it protects lives when shaking starts and works with no warning.
Add a limit: it is expensive, so poorer countries cannot build all homes this way.
Compare to another strategy: planning such as drills and evacuation costs less but does not stop collapse.
Make a judgement: it is the most effective, but best combined with planning in poorer places.
model.answer: I partly agree. Earthquake-proof building is very effective because it saves lives even without warning. However it is expensive, so poorer countries cannot afford it for all homes. Cheaper methods such as practice drills are less effective alone, so the best approach combines building design with planning.

teach.note: I do. Evaluation questions need an argument for, an argument against, and a clear judgement. Many pupils stop after a for-and-against list. Teach the judgement stem: 'Overall, ... because ...'. Reuse in the 6- and 9-mark questions in the exam.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is a secondary effect of an earthquake?
options: Fire caused by broken gas pipes
A new building code being written
check.why: B follows from the primary shaking. A is primary. C is an immediate response and D is a long-term response.

teach.note: Answer: B. Pupils who chose C or D have mixed effects with responses; revisit the table.

practice: Sort these into primary / secondary effect or immediate / long-term response: landslide, search and rescue, rebuilding schools, people killed by collapsing buildings, cholera outbreak.
Give three reasons why people live near volcanoes.
independent: Core: State two ways of monitoring a volcano. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain why earthquakes are harder to predict than volcanic eruptions. (3 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate the use of monitoring, prediction, protection and planning in reducing the effects of a tectonic hazard. (6 marks)
exit: Define 'secondary effect' and give one example.
Return to the big question: give two reasons why people live near tectonic hazards.
lessons.homework: Research the Pacific Tsunami Warning system or Japanese earthquake drills and write 100 words on how it reduces risk.
lessons.send: SEND: colour-coded sort cards for effects and responses. EAL: bilingual keyword mat. Stretch: judge which strategy matters most for a low-income country and justify it.

lessons.title: Tectonic case studies: Nepal 2015 and Christchurch 2011 compared
lessons.bigQuestion: Does a country's wealth decide how much a tectonic disaster hurts?
objectives: Describe the causes, effects and responses of the 2015 Nepal earthquake (low-income country)
Describe the causes, effects and responses of the 2011 Christchurch earthquake (high-income country)
Compare the two events and explain the differences
successCriteria: All: state the place, date, magnitude and at least two effects for each earthquake
Most: compare responses using specific facts
Some: explain the differences by linking to levels of development, not only the size of the earthquake
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: comparing death tolls and magnitudes; Science: the energy of magnitude scales
lessons.smsc: Moral and social: solidarity with people in disaster, and the role of aid; understanding that suffering is not equal

keywords.def: the energy released by an earthquake, measured on the moment magnitude scale
when shaking turns wet ground into a liquid-like mud
a smaller earthquake that follows the main shock
a country with low average income and limited resources
a country with high average income and many resources

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four types of plate margin and one place for each.
State two primary effects of an earthquake.
State two ways of reducing the effects of earthquakes.

teach.heading: Case study: Nepal earthquake, 2015

timeline.label: 25 April 2015
timeline.text: Magnitude 7.8 earthquake; epicentre near Barpak, Gorkha district, about 80 km north-west of Kathmandu; shallow focus

timeline.label: Effects
timeline.text: About 9,000 killed and about 22,000 injured; over 500,000 homes destroyed (approx.); Dharahara Tower collapsed; avalanche on Everest killed 19

timeline.label: 12 May 2015
timeline.text: Major aftershock, magnitude 7.3, caused more deaths and landslides

timeline.label: Immediate response
timeline.text: Nepalese army, India, China, the UK and many NGOs; tents, food and rescue teams; remote villages cut off by landslides

timeline.label: Long term
timeline.text: National Reconstruction Authority set up; rebuilding slow; new building rules; tourism damaged

teach.note: Cause: Nepal lies on the collision margin of the Indian and Eurasian plates. Nepal is a low-income country: dense hill villages built of stone and mud brick, little earthquake design, and few resources for rescue. Teach the figures as approximate and say so; the exact death toll differs by source. Ask: why did it take days for help to reach some villages? (Landslides blocked mountain roads; few helicopters; poor infrastructure.) Treat with sensitivity: this was a real tragedy, and many people were bereaved.

teach.heading: Case study: Christchurch earthquake, 2011

timeline.label: 22 February 2011
timeline.text: Magnitude 6.3; focus shallow (about 5 km); epicentre about 10 km from the city centre; New Zealand sits on the Pacific and Australian plate margin

timeline.label: Effects
timeline.text: 185 people killed (115 in the CTV building collapse); about 100,000 homes damaged; liquefaction flooded streets; city centre cordoned off

timeline.label: Economic cost
timeline.text: Around NZ$40 billion (approx.), mostly insured

timeline.label: Immediate response
timeline.text: Local and international rescue teams; shelters; water and power restored within days to weeks

timeline.label: Long term
timeline.text: Insurance paid for rebuilding; new building rules; city centre rebuilt over a decade

teach.note: Link to magnitude: this earthquake was smaller (6.3) than Nepal's (7.8) but caused huge damage because it was shallow and near a city. New Zealand is a high-income country with strong building codes, so most people survived and most losses were insured. Note the 115 deaths in one building which had structural problems. Ask: what do the deaths in Christchurch tell us about the limits of wealth? Check dates and figures before the lesson; they are accurate to the best of the author's knowledge but approximations are marked approx.

teach.heading: Compare the two events

head: Feature
Nepal 2015 (LIC)
Christchurch 2011 (HIC)
rows: Slow in remote areas; relied on foreign help
Fast; trained local teams plus international teams
Funded largely by insurance; city rebuilt

teach.note: Ask pupils to look for the surprise: the bigger earthquake had the bigger toll, but Christchurch's smaller quake still caused heavy damage. Conclude: magnitude matters but development is the key difference in deaths and recovery. Do not say poorer countries have no capacity: Nepal had good community response. Remind pupils that the exam wants place-specific facts to be used inside an explanation.

teach.heading: Skill: a comparison paragraph

model.problem: Compare the effects of an earthquake in a low-income country and a high-income country. (4 marks)
steps: Compare, not list: use 'whereas', 'but' and 'however'.
Use a fact from each place: about 9,000 deaths in Nepal and 185 in Christchurch.
Give the reason: weaker buildings and slower emergency help in Nepal.
Close with the main similarity or difference as a judgement.
model.answer: The 2015 Nepal earthquake killed about 9,000 people, whereas the 2011 Christchurch earthquake killed 185. This is because Nepal is a low-income country with weaker buildings and fewer rescue resources, while New Zealand has strict building codes and trained rescue teams. However, both events destroyed many homes.

teach.note: I do. Underline the comparative words. Pupils often write two separate paragraphs and miss the comparison marks. Show how to join facts with 'whereas'.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Christchurch had a smaller magnitude than Nepal. What is the best explanation for its large damage?
options: The earthquake was shallow and close to a city
check.why: B is correct: shallow focus and nearness to people raise damage. A, C and D are false for New Zealand. Pupils choosing A have stereotyped wealth.

teach.note: Answer: B. Use it to show that the nature of the hazard interacts with human factors.

practice: Create a fact file for each earthquake: date, magnitude, cause, two primary effects, two secondary effects, two responses.
Mark each fact as 'nature of the hazard' or 'level of development'.
independent: Core: Give two primary effects of the earthquake in your chosen LIC or HIC case study. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how the responses to the two earthquakes differed. (4 marks)
Stretch: 'The wealth of a country is the most important factor in the damage caused by earthquakes.' Using two case studies, how far do you agree? (9 marks)
exit: Name one effect and one response for Nepal 2015.
Return to the big question: write one sentence on wealth and one on magnitude.
lessons.homework: Complete a one-page revision sheet on your two case studies with a checklist of place facts, then self-test with the table covered.
lessons.send: SEND: fact cards with highlighted numbers. EAL: key vocabulary and sentence stems for comparing. Stretch: add Tohoku 2011, Japan, as a third example and discuss the role of tsunamis.

lessons.unit: Unit 3: Weather hazards in the UK (AQA 3.1.1.3, UK strand; tropical storms are taught in the existing Unit 1 lessons)
lessons.title: UK weather hazards and extreme weather: the July 2022 heatwave
lessons.bigQuestion: Is the UK's weather becoming more extreme?
objectives: Outline the main UK weather hazards
Use evidence to judge whether UK weather is becoming more extreme
Describe the impacts of, and management response to, the July 2022 heatwave
successCriteria: All: name four UK weather hazards and one impact of each
Most: use two pieces of evidence to say whether weather is becoming more extreme
Some: assess how well the 2022 heatwave was managed
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading record temperature data; Science: heat and health
lessons.smsc: Moral: caring for the vulnerable in extreme weather, neighbour by neighbour

keywords.def: weather events well outside the normal range, such as record heat or rain
a prolonged period of unusually hot weather
a long period with much less rainfall than normal
when water covers land that is normally dry
the UK's national weather service that issues weather warnings

starter: Say Bismillah. What is the difference between weather and climate?
Name the two types of climate change cause: natural and human. Give one of each.
Define 'risk'.

teach.heading: UK weather hazards

head: Hazard
Typical season
Example impact
rows: Autumn and winter, also summer storms
Power cuts, fallen trees, ferry and train disruption
Health risks, wildfires, crop and water shortages
Travel chaos, schools closed, risk to the elderly

teach.note: Brainstorm first. This slide covers the outline of UK hazards in the spec; tropical storms have already been taught in this course, so do not repeat. Emphasise that the UK's temperate maritime climate rarely has extremes, so the country is not well prepared: roads and homes are built for cool, wet weather, not 40 degrees. Ask: why does a small amount of snow cause such disruption? (Little equipment and planning, because it is rare.)

teach.heading: Evidence: record UK temperatures

timeline.text: Cheltenham: 37.1 °C (approx.)
Faversham, Kent: 38.5 °C
Cambridge Botanic Garden: 38.7 °C
Coningsby, Lincolnshire: 40.3 °C, the first time 40 °C was recorded in the UK

teach.note: Ask pupils what the pattern suggests (records are being broken more often). Add other evidence: the Met Office reports that the UK's warmest years have mostly occurred since 2002 (teacher to check the current list); winter 2013 to 2014 was the wettest on record for England and Wales (approx. record series from 1766); Storm Desmond in December 2015 set a new UK 24-hour rainfall record (about 341 mm at Honister Pass, Cumbria). Counter-point for balance: weather varies naturally, and a few records do not prove a trend. Climate scientists link the pattern to climate change.

teach.heading: Case study: July 2022 heatwave

head: Feature
Detail
rows: 18 to 19 July 2022; England worst; 40.3 °C at Coningsby on 19 July
First ever Red warning for extreme heat from the Met Office
Heat-related deaths estimated at about 3,000 for summer 2022 in England (approx.)
Rail speed limits and cancellations; Luton Airport runway damage; fires in London, e.g. Wennington
Warnings; advice to stay indoors and check on elderly neighbours; hosepipe bans later in summer; drought declared in many areas in August

teach.note: Ask pupils which impacts are primary and which secondary. Cause: a plume of hot air from Spain and the Sahara pushed north under a high-pressure system. Management happens before (forecasts and warnings), during (advice, services) and after (drought measures, review). Ask: how well prepared was the UK? Pupils can use evidence both ways. Death estimates vary by report; check the current UKHSA figure before teaching and say 'about'.

teach.heading: Skill: use evidence for a view

model.problem: 'UK weather is becoming more extreme.' Use evidence to support this view. (3 marks)
steps: Make a claim: records are being broken.
Add a precise piece of evidence: 40.3 °C recorded in July 2022, higher than the 2019 record of 38.7 °C.
Link evidence to the claim: higher records more often suggest greater extremes.
Add one more piece of evidence or a balance point.
model.answer: The evidence suggests that UK weather is becoming more extreme. In July 2022 the UK recorded 40.3 °C for the first time, higher than the previous record of 38.7 °C in 2019, which shows temperature records are being broken. In winter 2013 to 2014 England and Wales also had record rainfall.

teach.note: I do. Show how a number turns a vague statement into a mark. Stress that evidence must be specific. Invite a balance point: a few records do not prove a trend.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is the best example of a long-term response to a heatwave?
options: A Red warning from the Met Office
A review of rail networks to cope with higher temperatures
check.why: C is long-term planning. A and D are immediate; B is a short-term management measure during drought.

teach.note: Answer: C. This links to the same vocabulary in tectonics: immediate versus long-term.

practice: List UK weather hazards and for each give one economic and one social impact.
Make a spider diagram of the impacts of the 2022 heatwave, using different colours for primary and secondary.
independent: Core: Give two UK weather hazards. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain two impacts of a recent UK extreme weather event you have studied. (4 marks)
Stretch: Assess the evidence that UK weather is becoming more extreme. (6 marks)
exit: State one piece of evidence that UK temperatures are changing.
Return to the big question: give one reason for and one reason against.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word summary: 'How did the UK respond to the July 2022 heatwave?' Include at least two facts.
lessons.send: SEND: highlighted fact cards and sentence stems. EAL: weather vocabulary with pictures. Stretch: compare the 2022 heatwave with a flood event such as Storm Desmond.

lessons.unit: Autumn 2: Fragile environments and climate change (7.1 to 7.3, Paper 2 Section C)
lessons.title: Climate change: natural causes and the enhanced greenhouse effect (7.1)
lessons.bigQuestion: If the climate has always changed naturally, why worry now?
objectives: To understand the natural causes of climate change and how human activity enhances the greenhouse effect
successCriteria: All: name three natural causes of climate change
Most: explain the greenhouse effect and how humans enhance it
Some: evaluate the evidence that recent change is mainly human-caused
lessons.crossCurricular: Chemistry: the atmosphere and greenhouse gases
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility for the atmosphere and future generations

keywords.def: gases in the atmosphere trapping heat and keeping Earth warm
extra warming from greenhouse gases added by people
regular changes in Earth's orbit and tilt that affect climate
a greenhouse gas released by burning fossil fuels
a strong greenhouse gas from cattle, rice fields and landfill

hook.text: Without any greenhouse effect, Earth would be frozen. So is the greenhouse effect good or bad?

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'He raised the sky and set up the balance, so that you do not transgress the balance' (ar-Rahman 55:7 to 8). The atmosphere is part of that balance. Upsetting it through waste and excess goes against Islamic teaching, and Muslims are urged not to waste (al-A'raf 7:31).

starter.q: Which is a cause of desertification?
The Sahel is south of the:

teach.heading: Natural causes
bullets: Large volcanic eruptions cool the Earth briefly
teach.note: Milankovitch cycles work over tens of thousands of years and explain ice ages. The 1991 Pinatubo eruption cooled the world for a year or two.

teach.heading: The greenhouse effect
bullets: Greenhouse gases trap some of it
teach.note: Natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth about 33 °C warmer than it would be.

teach.heading: The enhanced greenhouse effect
teach.note: CO2 was about 280 parts per million before industry; it was above 420 ppm in the 2020s.

teach.heading: Natural or human?
bullets: Natural causes are slow or short-lived
Scientists conclude it is mainly human
teach.note: Global average temperature was roughly 1.1 to 1.3 °C above pre-industrial levels in the early 2020s.

teach.heading: Check
teach.note: Share results.

check.q: Which is a human cause of climate change?
check.why: Fossil fuel burning adds CO2; the others are natural.

practice.q: Explain how farming can enhance the greenhouse effect. (3 marks)
practice.a: Cattle and rice paddies release methane (1), a powerful greenhouse gas (1), which traps more heat in the atmosphere (1); clearing land also releases CO2
practice.model:
Name the activity: cattle farming.
Name the gas: methane.
Explain the effect: methane traps heat strongly, so more warming.

practice.q: Identify one natural cause that cools the climate for a short time. (1 mark)
practice.a: Large volcanic eruptions (ash and sulphur in the atmosphere)

practice.q: Using the chart, by how much did CO2 rise from before 1750 to the 2020s? (1 mark)
practice.a: About 140 ppm (280 to 420)

independent.q: Core: 'Explain how human activity enhances the greenhouse effect.' (6 marks) Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: Natural greenhouse effect explained; fossil fuels add CO2; deforestation reduces absorption; farming and landfill add methane; more gases trap more heat; reference to rising CO2 data
independent.model: Teacher plans it first: P1 the natural effect; P2 fossil fuels and CO2 with data; P3 deforestation; P4 methane from farming and landfill; conclusion: more gases, more heat trapped.

independent.q: Extend: 'Evaluate the view that recent climate change is mainly caused by natural factors.' (8 marks) Plan in bullet points.
independent.a: Natural factors act slowly (Milankovitch) or briefly (volcanoes) and solar output has not risen enough; rapid rise in CO2 matches warming; judgement: mainly human

independent.q: Stretch: Why do scientists use ice cores to study past climate? (2 marks)
independent.a: Air bubbles trapped in ice show past CO2 levels (1); layers show temperature changes over hundreds of thousands of years (1)

exit.q: Methane comes mainly from:
exit.a: Cattle, rice fields and landfill

exit.q: Big question: if the climate has always changed naturally, why worry now?
exit.a: Today's change is far faster than natural change and is mainly caused by human greenhouse gases, threatening fragile environments and people
