lessons.title: Climate change: effects, mitigation and adaptation
lessons.bigQuestion: Should we focus on stopping climate change or on adapting to it?
objectives: Give an overview of effects of climate change on people and the environment
Explain mitigation: alternative energy, carbon capture, tree planting and international agreements
Explain adaptation: changing farming, managing water supply and reducing risk from rising sea levels
successCriteria: All: give two effects and one mitigation and one adaptation strategy
Most: explain how each strategy works
Some: evaluate mitigation against adaptation and make a judgement
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: renewable energy and carbon capture; Economics: costs and benefits
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship, and fairness to countries that contribute least but suffer most

keywords.def: action to reduce the causes of climate change
action to cope with the effects of climate change
trapping carbon dioxide from power stations and storing it underground
energy from sources that do not run out, such as wind and solar
the increase in average sea level as ice melts and oceans warm

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two human causes of climate change.
What is the greenhouse effect?
Give one piece of evidence that the climate is changing.

teach.heading: Effects of climate change

head: Area
People
Environment
rows: Coastal flooding, loss of land and homes
Melting glaciers, ice sheets; rising sea level
More heatwaves, floods and droughts; damage to homes
Changing rainfall and more extreme storms
Coral bleaching; species moving or dying out

teach.note: Do not present all effects as certain at every location: some places may get wetter, others drier. Ask pupils which groups are most vulnerable: low-lying nations such as Bangladesh and Pacific islands. Link to earlier lessons on capacity to cope. Teach the term 'overview': the spec wants a broad picture, not a case study.

teach.heading: Two responses

left.title: Mitigation: tackle the cause
points: International agreements: Kyoto (1997) and Paris (2015) set emissions targets

right.title: Adaptation: cope with the effects
points: Farming: drought-resistant crops, changing planting dates
Water supply: reservoirs, rainwater harvesting, reducing waste
Sea-level risk: sea walls, raised homes, barriers such as the Thames Barrier

teach.note: Make the distinction crisp: mitigation attacks the cause, adaptation lives with the effect. Pupils swap them regularly. Paris Agreement 2015: nations aim to keep warming well below 2 °C and pursue 1.5 °C. Ask for strengths and limits of each: mitigation needs cooperation between countries; adaptation is local and quick but does not stop the cause. Thames Barrier opened in 1982 to protect London from tidal surges.

teach.heading: Strategy evaluation

head: Strategy
Strength
Weakness
rows: Costly to build; some depend on weather
Allows continued use of fossil fuels with fewer emissions
Expensive; storage sites needed; not yet widespread
Slow; trees take years to grow
Cost; does not stop climate change

teach.note: Use this table as a bank of evaluation material: strength and weakness for each. Ask pupils which strategy they would choose if they were an adviser to a low-income country, and why. Stress there is no single right answer; the mark is for the reasoning and the judgement. Weigh cost, speed, effectiveness and fairness.

teach.heading: Skill: a balanced judgement

model.problem: Evaluate the success of mitigation and adaptation as ways of managing climate change. (6 marks, outline)
steps: Argument for mitigation: it addresses the cause so benefits are long-term and global.
Argument against: it needs international agreement and is slow to deliver results.
Argument for adaptation: it protects people now, for example flood barriers.
Judgement: both are needed; mitigation is more important over time but adaptation protects the vulnerable now.
model.answer: Mitigation, such as the Paris Agreement, tackles the cause and so could benefit everyone in the long term, but it needs countries to cooperate. Adaptation, such as raised homes in coastal areas, protects people straight away but does not stop climate change. Overall a combination is best because mitigation reduces future risk and adaptation protects people now.

teach.note: I do. Use the structure: argue, counter, judge. Students find the judgement hardest, so give a stem: 'Overall, ... is more important because ...'.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is an example of adaptation?
options: Building flood barriers in a coastal town
check.why: C copes with sea-level rise. A, B and D reduce the causes.

teach.note: Answer: C. If a pupil chooses B, ask whether planting trees stops a flood or removes carbon dioxide.

practice: Sort strategies into mitigation or adaptation: solar farm, drought-resistant crops, tree planting, sea wall, Paris Agreement, rainwater harvesting.
Write one strength and one weakness for each of carbon capture and sea walls.
independent: Core: State the difference between mitigation and adaptation. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how people can adapt to the risk of sea-level rise. (4 marks)
Stretch: 'Mitigation is more important than adaptation.' How far do you agree? (6 marks)
exit: Name one mitigation and one adaptation strategy.
Return to the big question: take a side and give one reason.
lessons.homework: Write a letter to a politician explaining which climate strategy you would prioritise, with two reasons. About 150 words.
lessons.send: SEND: sorting cards and sentence frame 'Mitigation is... whereas adaptation is...'. EAL: key terms in home language. Stretch: research one country's climate adaptation plan.

lessons.title: Ecosystems: food webs, nutrient cycling, biomes and a UK woodland
lessons.bigQuestion: What happens to a whole ecosystem when just one part changes?
objectives: Explain producers, consumers, decomposers, food chains, food webs and nutrient cycling
Show how changing one component affects the balance of the system
Describe the distribution of the main global biomes and a small-scale UK ecosystem
successCriteria: All: label a food chain and name the roles of producers, consumers and decomposers
Most: explain the effect of changing one part of a food web or nutrient cycle
Some: use a case study to show interdependence in an ecosystem and link biomes to climate
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: food webs, photosynthesis and decay
lessons.smsc: Spiritual and moral: balance (mizan) in creation; our responsibility not to disturb it carelessly

keywords.def: a community of living things and the non-living environment they interact with
an organism that makes its own food, such as a plant
an organism that eats other living things
an organism that breaks down dead material and returns nutrients to the soil
linked food chains showing feeding relationships
a large-scale ecosystem with similar climate, plants and animals

starter: Say Bismillah. What do plants need for photosynthesis?
What is a food chain? Give an example of three links.
What happens to leaves when they fall and rot?

teach.heading: Parts of an ecosystem
bullets: Producers make food by photosynthesis, such as oak trees and grass.
Consumers eat plants or animals, such as mice and owls.
Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, break down dead matter.
Non-living parts: climate, soil, water and rock.
teach.note: Start from a pupil's local park or woodland and have them name living and non-living parts. Draw a woodland food chain: oak leaf, caterpillar, blue tit, sparrowhawk. A food web links many chains. Stress arrows show the flow of energy, pointing from the eaten to the eater: the common mistake is arrows pointing the wrong way. Ecosystems vary in size: a pond is small-scale, a biome is large-scale.

teach.heading: Nutrient cycle in a woodland
cycle: Trees take up nutrients from the soil
Nutrients are stored in leaves, branches and trunk
Leaf fall adds litter to the ground
teach.note: In the Gersmehl model nutrients move between three stores: biomass, litter and soil. Ask which store is largest in a temperate woodland (soil and litter hold a lot) compared with a rainforest (biomass). This idea returns in the rainforest lesson. Misconception: soils contain endless nutrients; if the cycle is broken, for example by removing the litter or cutting the trees, the nutrients are lost. Link to mizan: the system works because each part does its job.

teach.heading: Skill: explain a change in a food web

model.problem: A pond food web includes algae, water fleas, small fish and herons. Pollution kills most of the water fleas. Explain the effect on the pond. (4 marks)
steps: Direct effect: the small fish lose a food source, so they decline.
Knock-on effect: with fewer small fish, herons have less to eat.
Opposite effect: algae, no longer eaten, may increase and block light.
State that one change disrupts balance through the whole web.
model.answer: If water fleas die, small fish have less food so their numbers fall. This means herons have less to eat and may move away. Algae are eaten less so they may grow rapidly and block light, which shows that changing one part upsets the balance of the whole ecosystem.

teach.note: I do. Show how arrows in the food web give the chain of reasoning. Ask: what would happen if the herons were removed instead? Pupils practise predicting both increases and decreases; many only predict decreases.

teach.heading: Global biomes

head: Biome
Location
Climate and plants
rows: Hot and wet all year; dense evergreen forest
Either side of rainforests (e.g. East Africa)
Warm with wet and dry seasons; grass and scattered trees
About 20 to 30 degrees north and south (e.g. Sahara)
Mild, rain all year; trees lose leaves in winter
Very cold; low plants, frozen ground

teach.note: Show a world map. Pupils colour in biomes to see that climate controls the biome: temperature and rainfall decide which plants can grow, and plants decide which animals live there. Ask: why are deserts found near 30 degrees north and south? (Sinking dry air, linked to atmospheric circulation covered earlier.) Boreal coniferous forest (taiga) may also be mentioned between the temperate forests and tundra.

teach.heading: Case study: a UK woodland, e.g. Epping Forest (or a local wood)
teach.note: Choose a named woodland: use Epping Forest (Essex and Greater London) as the example or the teacher's local woodland or a pond if fieldwork has been done there. Use the table to talk about interdependence: the oak supports hundreds of insect species, which feed birds, which feed predators such as tawny owls and sparrowhawks. Fungi and bacteria recycle leaf litter. Ask what would happen if deer numbers soared (grazing could remove the bluebells and young trees). Check any named site facts before teaching; the table is general.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: In a food web, what do the arrows show?
options: The direction of energy flow, from the food to the eater
check.why: Arrows point from the organism being eaten to the one that eats it, showing energy transfer.

teach.note: Answer: B. A common error is to point the arrow from the predator to the prey.

practice: Draw a food web for a woodland using at least six organisms and label producers, consumers and decomposers.
Predict what happens if rabbits are removed from your web.
independent: Core: Define the term 'decomposer'. (1 mark) Give one example. (1 mark)
Extend: Explain how a change in one part of an ecosystem affects the others. (4 marks)
Stretch: Using a named UK ecosystem, explain how the plants, animals and soil depend on each other. (6 marks)
exit: Which biome is found near the equator?
Return to the big question: give one example of a change causing a chain of effects.
lessons.homework: Draw a nutrient cycle for a woodland or pond and explain what would happen if all the decomposers died. About 100 words.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-drawn food web with cut-out organisms to arrange. EAL: labelled pictures for producer/consumer/decomposer. Stretch: link biome distribution to atmospheric circulation and ocean currents.

lessons.title: Tropical rainforests: climate, interdependence and adaptation
lessons.bigQuestion: How can the most species-rich ecosystem on Earth grow on poor soil?
objectives: Describe the physical characteristics of tropical rainforests
Explain how climate, soil, plants, animals and water interrelate
Explain plant and animal adaptations and why biodiversity is so high
successCriteria: All: describe the climate and the layers of the rainforest
Most: explain how the nutrient cycle and the soil are connected to the climate and plants
Some: explain adaptations and link them to the competition for light, food and survival
lessons.crossCurricular: Biology: adaptation and photosynthesis
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on the diversity and complexity of creation as signs for those who reflect

keywords.def: the variety of plant and animal species in a place
the dense layer of treetops, about 25 to 45 m above the ground
the tallest trees that rise above the canopy
a plant that grows on another plant, using it for light without harming it
a feature that helps an organism survive in its environment

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the biome near the equator and two features of its climate.
Explain what a decomposer does.
Describe what happens to nutrients when a leaf falls.

teach.heading: Climate and location

head: Feature
Tropical rainforest
rows: Within about 10 degrees of the equator: Amazon, Congo, Southeast Asia
About 26 to 28 °C all year (approx.); little seasonal change
Over 2,000 mm a year; rain nearly every day
Evergreen trees in layers; dense growth

teach.note: Link the climate to the equatorial low-pressure belt: the Sun is high, air rises, and convection rain falls daily. Use Manaus, Brazil as a data point if the class has done climate graphs: about 27 °C and about 2,300 mm rain a year (approx.). Ask pupils to describe, not explain, and then ask them to explain why the growth is so fast (heat, water, light all year).

teach.heading: Interdependence: climate to soil
cycle: Hot, wet climate gives rapid plant growth
Dead leaves fall and decompose in weeks
Nutrients are taken up quickly by shallow roots
Most nutrients are held in plants, not soil
Soil is thin and nutrient-poor; heavy rain washes nutrients out
teach.note: Stress the paradox: lush forest on poor soil. The forest survives because the nutrients are recycled so fast they do not stay in the soil. This also explains why cleared forest soon becomes infertile, which we use in the next lesson. Ask pupils which store in the Gersmehl model is largest here (biomass) and which is smallest (litter, since it decays so fast, and soil).

teach.heading: Adaptations

left.title: Plants
points: Buttress roots support tall trees on thin soil
Epiphytes grow on branches to reach light
Lianas climb up trees using them for support

right.title: Animals
points: Camouflage, such as sloths covered in algae
Warning colours, such as poison dart frogs
Long limbs and prehensile tails for climbing
Many are nocturnal or live in specific layers

teach.note: Ask pupils to link each adaptation to the problem it solves: waterlogged leaves, lack of light, predators. Biodiversity: over half of the world's land plant and animal species may live in rainforests (a commonly quoted estimate; treat as approx.). Competition for light and food drives specialisation, and niches in each layer create a huge range of species. Emphasise to pupils that adaptation takes place over generations; individual animals do not adapt in their lifetimes.

teach.heading: Skill: explain an adaptation

model.problem: Explain how one adaptation helps a plant to survive in a rainforest. (3 marks)
steps: Name the adaptation: buttress roots.
Say what it does: they spread out at the base of tall trees.
Link to the problem: the soil is thin, so they stop the tree falling over.
model.answer: Many rainforest trees have buttress roots. These spread widely at the base of the trunk, so they give support in thin, shallow soil, which stops the tall trees falling over in heavy rain and wind.

teach.note: I do. Three marks means name, describe, explain. Pupils often just name the adaptation. Ask them to rehearse with drip tips: it lets heavy rain run off quickly so the leaf does not grow mould or break.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Why is the soil in a tropical rainforest often poor in nutrients?
options: Nutrients are quickly taken up by plants and washed out by heavy rain
check.why: Rapid recycling holds nutrients in biomass, and rainfall washes the surplus out. Decomposers are active, not absent.

teach.note: Answer: B. Pupils choosing C mix up cause and effect: decomposition is fast, which is why little litter builds up.

practice: Draw and label the layers of a rainforest with the typical height of each.
Match each adaptation to the problem it solves.
independent: Core: Describe the climate of a tropical rainforest. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how rainforest plants are adapted to the conditions. (4 marks)
Stretch: Explain how climate, soils, plants and animals are interdependent in the rainforest. (6 marks)
exit: Name two adaptations of rainforest animals.
Return to the big question: summarise in one sentence why rainforest soil is poor.
lessons.homework: Create a labelled poster of a rainforest food web showing at least three adaptations.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-labelled rainforest layers diagram. EAL: pictures and bilingual labels for adaptations. Stretch: explain why biodiversity is greater in rainforests than in temperate forests.

lessons.title: Deforestation in the Amazon: rates, causes and impacts
lessons.bigQuestion: Who gains and who loses when the rainforest is cleared?
objectives: Describe changing rates of deforestation in the Amazon, Brazil
Explain causes: farming, logging, road building, mineral extraction, energy and settlement
Assess the impacts on economic development, soil erosion and climate change
successCriteria: All: name three causes of deforestation and one impact
Most: use figures from the Amazon to describe changing rates and explain causes
Some: assess both benefits and costs and reach a judgement
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics: costs, benefits and opportunity cost; Maths: describing change over time
lessons.smsc: Moral: weighing short-term profit against the trust (amanah) we hold for future generations

keywords.def: the permanent removal of forest, mostly for farming, logging and building
raising cattle on large areas of cleared land
the removal of topsoil by wind or water
cutting only the most valuable trees
washing of nutrients out of the soil by rain

starter: Say Bismillah. Why is rainforest soil low in nutrients?
Describe one adaptation of a rainforest plant.
Name one human cause of climate change.

teach.heading: Changing rates: Brazilian Amazon

timeline.label: 1970s
timeline.text: Roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway open the forest to settlers and ranchers
Peak: about 27,800 km² cleared in one year (approx.)
Low: about 4,600 km² (approx.) after tougher enforcement and satellite monitoring
Rises again: about 13,000 km² (approx.)

timeline.label: Overall
timeline.text: About 17% of the Brazilian Amazon forest has been lost (approx.)

teach.note: Rates are a question of change over time; they are not constant, because policy and prices matter. Teach pupils to describe the trend with figures: falling by more than 80 per cent between 2004 and 2012, then rising again. Figures are annual estimates of the Brazilian space agency satellite programme and are approximate; teacher to check against the latest data. The 17 per cent is often quoted as an estimate for total loss of the Brazilian Amazon since the 1970s; label as approx.

teach.heading: Causes of deforestation

head: Cause
How it clears forest
rows: Largest cause in Brazil: forest cleared and burned for pasture
Soya and other crops grown for export and animal feed
Legal and illegal timber extraction; logging roads open the forest
Roads such as the BR-163 and the Trans-Amazonian Highway bring settlers
Iron ore and gold mines; hydroelectric dams such as Belo Monte flood forest
Poor farmers and growing towns clear land for housing and subsistence farming

teach.note: Ask pupils to rank causes by their importance. Note that some causes work together: roads allow loggers in; loggers allow ranchers in. Be fair: many people clearing land are poor families seeking a living, and also large companies. Check pupils' understanding by asking which causes are commercial and which are subsistence.

teach.heading: Soil erosion after clearance
cycle: Bare soil is hit by heavy rain
Topsoil and nutrients are washed away
Rivers silt up; land loses fertility
Farms are abandoned and more forest is cleared
teach.note: Draw this on the board. The cycle shows why cleared land is often productive only for a few years, which pushes farmers to clear more. Link to the interdependence lesson: without trees there is no leaf litter and the nutrient cycle breaks. Ask: what other effects arise from silt in rivers? (Fish habitats are damaged.)

teach.heading: Impacts of deforestation

left.title: Benefits
points: Jobs and income from ranching, farming and mining

right.title: Costs
points: Soil erosion and loss of fertility
Less carbon dioxide absorbed; burning releases it; less rainfall locally
Loss of homes and culture for indigenous peoples

teach.note: Ask for a view: whose benefits and whose costs? Link the climate impact: trees store carbon, so cutting and burning them adds carbon dioxide; fewer trees means less water released to the air (transpiration), so less rain may fall. The spec expects an assessment, which means weighing. Possible judgement: benefits are short-term and uneven; costs are long-term and global.

teach.heading: Skill: case-study paragraph

model.problem: Using the Amazon rainforest, explain two causes of deforestation. (4 marks)
steps: Cause 1 with detail: cattle ranching, where forest is burned for pasture in Brazil.
Explain why: beef is a valuable export, so there is strong demand for land.
Cause 2 with detail: roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway, opened in the 1970s.
Explain why: roads allow settlers, loggers and farmers into the forest.
model.answer: One cause is cattle ranching because large areas of forest in Brazil are burned for pasture and beef is a valuable export. Another cause is road building, as roads such as the Trans-Amazonian Highway let settlers and loggers enter the forest and clear land.

teach.note: I do. Case-study questions always need a named place and a place fact. Highlight the specific words. Pupils often write generic causes with no Amazon detail, and so lose marks.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Why does soil erosion increase after trees are cut down?
options: Roots hold soil and leaves shelter it from rain, and without them rain hits bare soil
check.why: Removing trees exposes soil and removes the roots that bind it, so heavy rain washes it away.

teach.note: Answer: A.

practice: Describe the trend in Amazon deforestation using the figures from 2004, 2012 and 2021.
Complete a table of causes with one Amazon fact for each.
independent: Core: State two causes of deforestation in the Amazon. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how deforestation can lead to soil erosion. (3 marks)
Stretch: Assess the impacts of deforestation on people and the environment in a named rainforest area. (6 marks)
exit: State one economic benefit of deforestation and one cost.
Return to the big question: name one group who gain and one who lose.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word letter from a rancher and from an indigenous leader about deforestation to compare views.
lessons.send: SEND: causes sorting cards with Amazon facts. EAL: key terms with visuals. Stretch: use rate figures to calculate the percentage fall between 2004 and 2012.

lessons.title: Why the rainforest matters and how to manage it sustainably
lessons.bigQuestion: Can the rainforest be used without being destroyed?
objectives: Explain the value of rainforests to people and the environment
Describe sustainable management strategies: selective logging, conservation, ecotourism, hardwood agreements and debt reduction
Evaluate which strategies are most effective in the Amazon
successCriteria: All: give two reasons why rainforests are valuable and name two strategies
Most: explain how each strategy helps to protect the forest
Some: evaluate strategies and make a justified recommendation
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics: debt and trade; Science: carbon stores
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship and justice for indigenous peoples; balancing needs of the poor and the planet

keywords.def: using resources so they will still be available to future generations
protecting and looking after nature
tourism that protects the environment and benefits local people
an agreement to buy only timber from sustainable sources
cancelling debt in return for protecting the environment

starter: Say Bismillah. Name three causes of deforestation.
What is soil erosion?
Give one benefit and one cost of deforestation.

teach.heading: Why rainforests matter

left.title: People
points: Homes and culture of indigenous peoples
Food, timber, rubber, medicines and nuts

right.title: Environment
points: Home to about half of the world's species (approx.)
Release water vapour that affects the climate

teach.note: Ask pupils which value matters most to local people and which matters to the world. Emphasise that carbon storage gives the forest global value: when it is burned, carbon dioxide is released. Many modern medicines were originally developed from plants. Take care with statistics: do not claim rainforests are the 'lungs of the Earth', which is misleading as the forest uses most of the oxygen it produces.

teach.heading: Sustainable management strategies

head: Strategy
How it works
Strength
Weakness
rows: Only mature trees cut; canopy and young trees left
Reserves and indigenous territories protected by law
Visitors pay to see forest; money supports local people
Gives forest a value without clearing
Can damage if too many visit
Countries buy only timber from certified sources
Debt cancelled in return for protecting forest
Reduces pressure to sell forest resources

teach.note: Take each strategy and check what it does; the weakness column prepares pupils for evaluation. Debt-for-nature swaps began in 1987 when a conservation group bought part of Bolivia's debt. Brazil's protected areas and indigenous territories now cover a large share of the Amazon (check the current percentage before teaching). The Amazon Fund, set up in 2008 and supported by Norway and Germany, pays for forest protection. Keep the notes brief and focus on the exam skill.

teach.heading: Skill: evaluate sustainable management

model.problem: Evaluate the effectiveness of ecotourism and conservation in protecting the Amazon rainforest. (6 marks, outline)
steps: Ecotourism: gives income to local people and so reduces the need to clear land.
Limit: too many tourists damage trails and wildlife, and income is small compared with ranching.
Conservation: protected areas legally prevent clearance.
Limit and judgement: protected areas need enforcement; overall conservation is stronger but needs local income from ecotourism.
model.answer: Ecotourism gives local people an income without cutting trees, but the money is small compared with cattle ranching. Conservation areas protect the forest by law, but only if the law is enforced. Overall conservation is more effective, though it works best when local people also benefit from ecotourism.

teach.note: I do. Pupils must show a judgement and a reason. Remind them to name the Amazon in their answer. In 6-mark questions explanations should be developed, not just listed.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which strategy rewards a country for protecting forest by reducing what it owes?
check.why: Debt reduction (a debt-for-nature swap) cancels debt in return for conservation.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Complete the strategies table with a strength and weakness for each.
Rank the strategies from most to least effective and explain your choice.
independent: Core: Give two reasons why rainforests are valuable. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how selective logging can be sustainable. (3 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate the success of sustainable management strategies in a named rainforest area. (6 marks)
exit: State one strategy to manage rainforest sustainably and one weakness.
Return to the big question: answer yes or no and give a reason.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word proposal for a sustainable use of the rainforest to present to a council.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-filled table with cloze gaps. EAL: simple glossary with pictures. Stretch: evaluate how the Amazon Fund works and its limits.

lessons.unit: Unit 7: Cold environments (AQA 3.1.2.4; OPTION: hot deserts OR cold environments. Hot deserts are already taught in the existing Y10 Unit 2 lessons, so these cold-environment lessons are for classes or pupils taking that option)
lessons.title: Cold environments: tundra climate, permafrost and adaptation
lessons.bigQuestion: How can anything live where the ground is frozen for most of the year?
objectives: Describe the physical characteristics of the Arctic tundra
Explain links between climate, permafrost, soils, plants, animals and people
Explain plant and animal adaptations and why biodiversity is low
successCriteria: All: describe the climate and name three adaptations
Most: explain how permafrost affects soil, water and vegetation
Some: explain why cold environments are fragile and slow to recover
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: heat, freezing and adaptation
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on how life is sustained in even the harshest places

keywords.def: a cold treeless biome with low plants and frozen ground
ground that stays frozen for two or more years
the top layer of ground that thaws in summer
a feature that helps an organism to survive
easily damaged and slow to recover

starter: Say Bismillah. Name three biomes and one climate feature of each.
What is an adaptation? Give an example from the rainforest.
Why is biodiversity high in the rainforest?

teach.heading: Tundra location and climate

head: Feature
Arctic tundra
rows: North of the tree line, near the Arctic Circle: northern Alaska, Canada, Russia, Scandinavia
Winter below -30 °C is common; summer mean about 4 to 10 °C
Less than 250 mm a year, mostly snow: a cold desert
Up to 24 hours in summer and almost none in winter

teach.note: Use Utqiaġvik (Barrow), Alaska as a data point if you have a climate graph: an annual mean of around -12 °C and about 110 mm of precipitation (approx.). Explain that polar air is cold and dry and sinks, so little precipitation falls. The Antarctic is a polar desert and a different cold environment: for these lessons the case study is the Arctic tundra of Alaska, with Antarctica used in the third lesson.

teach.heading: Linked system
bullets: Cold climate keeps ground frozen as permafrost.
In summer the thin active layer thaws but cannot drain downwards.
Boggy, waterlogged, thin and acidic soils support low plants.
Few plants support few animals, so food chains are short.
teach.note: Draw a cross-section: active layer on top, permafrost beneath, which may be hundreds of metres deep (up to about 600 m at Prudhoe Bay, approx.). Water cannot drain through frozen ground, so the surface is marshy in summer. Ask pupils to say how people fit in: traditionally Inuit and Iñupiat hunting, fishing and herding. Link to the nutrient cycle: decay is slow in the cold, so nutrients are locked in dead matter. Remind pupils that cause and effect must be given in order.

teach.heading: Adaptations

left.title: Plants
points: Dark, hairy leaves absorb and hold heat, such as Arctic willow

right.title: Animals
points: Thick fur and fat, such as polar bear and musk ox
Seasonal colour change, such as Arctic fox and Arctic hare
Migration, such as caribou and many birds
Hibernation or reducing activity in winter

teach.note: Connect each adaptation to a problem: wind, cold, short growing season, camouflage. Note that biodiversity is low compared with the rainforest: few species can cope. Many species are specialists, so food chains are short and simple: if the number of one species falls, others are heavily affected. This also makes the environment fragile and slow to recover from damage, since plants take decades to regrow.

teach.heading: Skill: explain linkages

model.problem: Explain how permafrost affects vegetation in the tundra. (3 marks)
steps: Permafrost stops water draining, so the ground is boggy in summer.
Roots cannot penetrate the frozen layer, so plants are shallow-rooted and small.
Therefore trees cannot grow and vegetation is low mosses, lichens and grasses.
model.answer: Permafrost is frozen ground that water cannot drain through, so the soil is waterlogged in summer. Roots cannot grow deep, so only small, shallow-rooted plants such as mosses and lichens survive, and trees cannot grow.

teach.note: I do. Make the chain explicit with 'so' and 'because'. Most pupils say 'it is cold so nothing grows', which is too vague for the marks.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: What is the active layer?
options: The top layer of soil that thaws in summer
A layer of ice on lakes
check.why: The active layer thaws in summer above the permafrost. Pupils choosing A confuse it with the permafrost itself.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Draw a labelled cross-section of tundra ground showing the active layer and permafrost.
Match each adaptation to the problem it solves.
independent: Core: Describe the climate of the tundra. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how animals are adapted to the tundra. (4 marks)
Stretch: Explain how climate, permafrost, soil and vegetation are linked in the tundra. (6 marks)
exit: Define permafrost.
Return to the big question: give one animal and one plant adaptation.
lessons.homework: Make an adaptation fact-file for one Arctic animal and one plant, with a diagram.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled cross-section to complete. EAL: picture glossary with key terms. Stretch: compare adaptations of tundra and desert species.

lessons.unit: Unit 7: Cold environments (AQA 3.1.2.4; OPTION: hot deserts OR cold environments. Hot deserts are already taught in the existing Y10 Unit 2 lessons, so these cold-environment lessons are for classes or pupils taking that option)
lessons.title: Alaska's North Slope: opportunities and challenges of development
lessons.bigQuestion: Is it worth the effort to develop one of the coldest places on Earth?
objectives: Describe opportunities: mineral extraction, energy, fishing and tourism
Explain challenges: extreme temperatures, inaccessibility, and providing buildings and infrastructure
Use Alaska as a case study to show how technology overcomes challenges
successCriteria: All: give two opportunities and two challenges of developing a cold environment
Most: explain how permafrost thaw damages buildings and how engineers cope
Some: judge how successfully the Trans-Alaska Pipeline overcame the challenges
lessons.crossCurricular: Engineering: heat transfer and building design
lessons.smsc: Moral: weighing economic benefit against care for the land and for local peoples

keywords.def: the Arctic area of northern Alaska, including Prudhoe Bay oil field
difficult to reach, because of terrain or climate
roads, pipelines, buildings and services needed for development
uneven ground that forms when ice-rich permafrost thaws
a long tube that moves oil or gas

starter: Say Bismillah. What is permafrost?
Describe two adaptations of tundra plants.
Why is biodiversity low in cold environments?

teach.heading: Opportunities and challenges

head: Area
Opportunity
Challenge
rows: Oil and gas, coal, gold; hydro power
Extreme cold stops machines; permafrost sinks drills and pipes
Rich fisheries, such as pollock, salmon and crab off Alaska
Short season; costly access; fragile environment
Thawing ground causes buildings to sink; frozen pipes; few roads

teach.note: Link each opportunity to its matching challenge so that pupils practise 'Opportunity... but challenge...'. Tourism is a growing industry in Alaska, but locations such as the North Slope are remote. Extreme temperatures go to about -40 °C; metal becomes brittle, batteries fail, workers are at risk of frostbite and hypothermia. Inaccessible: few roads, so supplies come by air or ice roads. The Dalton Highway, built in the 1970s, runs about 666 miles (about 1,070 km) from Fairbanks to Deadhorse.

teach.heading: Case study: Trans-Alaska Pipeline

timeline.text: Huge oil field found at Prudhoe Bay on the North Slope

timeline.label: 1974 to 1977
timeline.text: Pipeline built, about 1,300 km (800 miles) from Prudhoe Bay to Valdez on the south coast

timeline.label: Design
timeline.text: About half of it raised above ground on supports with heat pipes so oil heat does not melt the permafrost
Exxon Valdez oil spill in Prince William Sound; a tanker, not the pipeline, but a warning about risk

timeline.label: Today
timeline.text: Oil income funds Alaska; output falling; debate about further drilling

teach.note: Explain why the pipeline is raised: the oil is warm, and if it were buried in ice-rich permafrost it would melt the ground, which would sink and break the pipe. Heat pipes (thermosyphons) draw heat from the supports. The route zigzags to allow for expansion and earthquake movement and has raised sections for caribou migration. Pipeline distance is about 1,287 km (approx.); proportion raised is about half (approx.); check. Ask pupils to weigh economic gain against risk.

teach.heading: Building in permafrost
bullets: Heated buildings melt the ground and sink.
Buildings are raised on piles so air can flow under.
Pipes for water and sewage are insulated and kept above ground.
Gravel pads spread weight and insulate the ground.
teach.note: Explain that thawed ground becomes mud and structures can crack or tilt. Climate change is also thawing permafrost, causing roads and buildings to subside in many Arctic settlements. Ask why building costs in Alaska are far higher than elsewhere (materials flown in, special foundations, short building season).

teach.heading: Skill: explain a challenge and solution

model.problem: Explain why building in permafrost areas is difficult and how engineers overcome this. (4 marks)
steps: Problem: heat from buildings melts the frozen ground.
Result: the ground becomes soft and the building sinks or cracks.
Solution: buildings and pipelines are built on stilts so air circulates.
Explain why this works: the ground under them stays frozen.
model.answer: Heat from buildings can melt the permafrost so the ground turns to mud and buildings sink or crack. Engineers build on stilts so cold air can flow under and keep the ground frozen, and they raise pipelines for the same reason.

teach.note: I do. Pupils often mention only the problem. Show how to add the solution and why it works. Give an Alaska example: parts of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline are raised.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Why are parts of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline raised above the ground?
options: So hot oil does not melt the permafrost beneath
To protect it from earthquakes only
To make it easier to paint
check.why: The oil is warm, so a buried pipe would melt the ground, which would sink. Raising on supports with heat pipes keeps the ground frozen.

teach.note: Answer: B. It also lets caribou migrate beneath.

practice: Complete the opportunity-and-challenge table for a cold environment using two facts from Alaska.
Explain with a diagram why buildings on stilts do not melt permafrost.
independent: Core: Give two challenges of developing cold environments. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how technology has helped development in a named cold environment. (4 marks)
Stretch: 'The opportunities of developing cold environments outweigh the challenges.' How far do you agree? Use a case study. (6 marks)
exit: Name one opportunity and one challenge in Alaska.
Return to the big question: give a view with one reason.
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word briefing to an oil company about the main risks of building a pipeline across permafrost.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled diagram of raised pipeline; cloze summary. EAL: key words with pictures. Stretch: research how climate warming now threatens infrastructure built on permafrost.

lessons.unit: Unit 7: Cold environments (AQA 3.1.2.4; OPTION: hot deserts OR cold environments. Hot deserts are already taught in the existing Y10 Unit 2 lessons, so these cold-environment lessons are for classes or pupils taking that option)
lessons.title: Wilderness, treaties and balancing development with conservation
lessons.bigQuestion: Who should decide what happens to the last wilderness places on Earth?
objectives: Explain the value of cold environments as wilderness
Explain why cold environments need protection
Evaluate technology, governments, treaties and conservation groups as ways to balance development and conservation
successCriteria: All: name two reasons cold environments are valuable and two ways of protecting them
Most: explain how the Antarctic Treaty and technology protect cold environments
Some: evaluate which approach is best
lessons.crossCurricular: Politics: international law and treaties; Science: polar research
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship; fairness between present and future generations and between nations

keywords.def: a large natural area little affected by people
protecting nature from damage
a formal agreement between countries
a 1959 agreement setting aside Antarctica for peaceful and scientific use
development that meets present needs without harming future generations

starter: Say Bismillah. State two opportunities in cold environments.
Why is infrastructure difficult to build on permafrost?
Define 'conservation'.

teach.heading: Value of cold environments

left.title: Why they matter
points: Wilderness: huge areas with few people
Habitats for polar bears, caribou, migrating birds
Scientific research: ice cores and climate data

right.title: Why they need protection
points: Oil spills and pipelines threaten wildlife
Tourism and ships bring waste and noise
Fragile: plants and animals recover slowly
Climate change is warming the Arctic faster than most places

teach.note: Draw out that value has several types: ecological, scientific, cultural (indigenous peoples) and aesthetic. Fragility is the key reason protection matters: damage lasts decades. The Arctic has warmed about two to four times faster than the global average in recent decades (approx. and varies by study; check). Ask pupils what 'wilderness' means to them and how it could be valued. Be careful not to imply no people live there: indigenous peoples have lived in the Arctic for thousands of years.

teach.heading: Strategies to balance development and conservation

head: Strategy
Example
Strength
Limit
rows: Raised pipelines; directional drilling reduces surface footprint
Cannot remove all risk; spills still happen
Protected areas in Alaska such as the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge
Laws and policy change with governments
Antarctic Treaty 1959; Madrid Protocol 1991 bans mining
Needs countries to agree and comply

teach.note: Dates: the Antarctic Treaty was signed in 1959 and came into force in 1961; it sets Antarctica aside for peaceful use and science. The Madrid Protocol was signed in 1991 and took effect in 1998; it bans mineral resource activities, with a review possible from 2048 (check wording). The Arctic has no equivalent treaty because it is mostly ocean surrounded by eight countries; the Arctic Council discusses cooperation. Ask pupils to say which strategy is hardest to enforce.

teach.heading: Skill: balanced judgement

model.problem: 'International treaties are the best way to protect cold environments.' How far do you agree? (6 marks, outline)
steps: For: treaties bind many countries, such as the Antarctic Treaty and its mining ban.
Against: treaties depend on countries agreeing and they have no real police; the Arctic has no such treaty.
Alternative: technology and conservation groups work at a local level.
Judgement: treaties are most powerful where there are no residents, but several approaches are needed.
model.answer: Treaties such as the Antarctic Treaty are effective because they bind many countries to peaceful use and a ban on mining. However they only work if countries comply, and the Arctic has no equivalent. Technology and conservation groups help locally, so overall treaties are powerful but need to be combined with other strategies.

teach.note: I do. The judgement must answer the 'how far' question. Insist on one sentence starting 'Overall'. Encourage a named example, such as the Antarctic Treaty or Alaska's refuge, for specific marks.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which strategy did the 1991 Madrid Protocol use to protect Antarctica?
check.why: The Protocol bans mining and sets rules on waste and wildlife, with a review no earlier than 2048.

teach.note: Answer: A.

practice: Sort the strategies into technology, governments, treaties or conservation groups, with an example for each.
Debate: 'Should Alaska allow more oil drilling?' with two arguments each side.
independent: Core: Give two reasons why cold environments need protecting. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how a treaty can protect a cold environment. (3 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate strategies for balancing development and conservation in a named cold environment. (6 marks)
exit: Name one treaty protecting a cold environment and one thing it does.
Return to the big question: write one sentence of your view.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word policy briefing recommending how to balance development and conservation in Alaska.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-completed strategies table with gaps. EAL: key terms in home language. Stretch: compare protection of the Arctic and Antarctic.

lessons.title: Where are the UK's uplands, lowlands and major rivers?
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do the north and west of the UK look so different from the south and east?
objectives: Locate the major upland and lowland areas of the UK
Locate the major river systems of the UK
Describe the pattern and link it to geology and the landscape studies that follow
successCriteria: All: name and locate three upland areas, three lowland areas and three rivers
Most: describe the pattern of relief using compass directions
Some: explain the pattern using rock type and glaciation
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths and skills: map reading, scale and height; Geology
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: awe at the variety of landscapes within one small country; stewardship of the land

keywords.def: high ground, usually over 200 m, with steep slopes
low, flatter land, usually below 200 m
a river and all its tributaries
where a river begins
where a river meets the sea or a lake

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four countries of the United Kingdom and their capitals.
What is a river's source and mouth?
Name one UK mountain and one UK river you know.

teach.heading: Upland and lowland UK

left.title: Upland: north and west
points: Hard, old rocks such as granite and slate
Steep slopes, thin soils, high rainfall
Mostly sheep farming, forestry and tourism
Shaped by ice during the last ice age

right.title: Lowland: south and east
points: Softer, younger rocks such as clay, chalk and sandstone
Gentle slopes, deep soils, drier and warmer
Many main rivers flow slowly across it

teach.note: Show a relief map and draw an imaginary diagonal line from the Tees to the Exe. North and west of it is mostly upland and older, harder rock; south and east lowland and younger, softer rock. This is a simplification: Scotland's Central Lowlands and Northern Ireland's Lough Neagh basin are lowland in the north and west, and the Chilterns and South Downs are low hills in the south. Ask pupils to find exceptions.

teach.heading: Major upland areas
teach.note: Ask pupils to place each area on a blank outline map as you speak. Mention Mourne Mountains in Northern Ireland (Slieve Donard, 850 m). Heights are rounded and should be checked by the teacher, but they are standard figures. Ask: which is the highest point in the UK? (Ben Nevis.) Ask: which uplands are in England? Point out that these places link to the glacial landscapes studied later.

teach.heading: Major rivers
teach.note: The Severn is the UK's longest river (about 354 km) and the Thames the second longest (about 346 km); the Tay carries the largest volume of water (approx.). Ask pupils what pattern they notice (most flow east, to the North Sea, because rain falls on the western hills and the land slopes to the east and south). Ensure pupils can say 'flows from the ... to the ...'.

teach.heading: Skill: describe a pattern on a map

model.problem: Describe the distribution of upland areas in the UK. (3 marks)
steps: Overall pattern: the uplands are mainly in the north and west.
Named examples: the Scottish Highlands, Pennines, Lake District and Snowdonia.
Contrast: south and east are mainly lowland, such as East Anglia.
Use compass directions.
model.answer: Most upland areas are in the north and west of the UK. Examples include the Scottish Highlands, the Pennines and Snowdonia. The south and east, such as East Anglia, are mainly low-lying.

teach.note: I do. Describe, do not explain. Give compass directions and named places. Pupils lose marks with 'in the north' alone.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which is the longest river in the UK?
check.why: The Severn is the longest. Pupils often choose the Thames because it is more famous.

teach.note: Answer: B. Use as a prompt to say why fame is not length.

practice: Label an outline map of the UK with five upland areas and five rivers.
Write two sentences describing the pattern of rivers on your map.

teach.heading: Changes downstream
teach.note: Draw a long profile as a smooth concave curve from steep to flat. Link channel size to discharge, which increases as tributaries join. Velocity usually increases downstream even though the gradient decreases, because the larger channel has less friction; pupils find this surprising. The Bradshaw model describes these changes: width, depth, discharge, velocity and load size. Ask: why is the load rounder downstream? (Attrition.)

teach.heading: Erosion and transport

left.title: Erosion
points: Hydraulic action: force of water in cracks
Abrasion: load scrapes the bed and banks
Attrition: stones collide and become smaller and rounder

right.title: Transport
points: Traction: large stones rolled along the bed
Saltation: smaller stones bounced along the bed
Suspension: fine silt carried in the water

teach.note: Pupils can match each process to the size of the load. In flood the river's energy is higher so it can move larger material. Deposition occurs when the river loses energy, for example when it floods, slows around a bend or enters the sea. Misconception: rivers only erode at the source. Erosion and deposition occur all the way along.

teach.heading: Skill: explain a downstream change

model.problem: Explain why the size of the river's load decreases downstream. (3 marks)
steps: Stones collide with each other and the bed: attrition.
This breaks them into smaller, rounder pieces.
Larger material is deposited when the river loses energy.
model.answer: Stones in the river are worn down by attrition as they collide with each other and the bed, so they get smaller and rounder as they move downstream. Heavy material is also deposited when the river's energy drops.

teach.note: I do. Each mark is a process-and-result pair. Pupils often say 'because it gets eroded' without naming attrition.

teach.note: Answer: B.

weathering when water freezes in cracks, expands and breaks rock
ice freezes to rock and pulls pieces away as it moves
rocks frozen in the ice scrape and scratch the valley
unsorted rock debris dropped by melting ice

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two UK upland areas.
Define 'weathering'.

teach.heading: The last ice age in the UK
bullets: The Devensian ice sheet peaked about 20,000 years ago (approx.).
Ice covered Scotland, Wales, northern England and parts of the Midlands.
Southern England was bitterly cold tundra.
Ice melted about 10,000 to 15,000 years ago.
teach.note: Show a map with the maximum extent of ice: it covered all of Scotland and most of Wales, with the south limit around the Bristol Channel in the west and North Norfolk coast in the east. Ice was up to a kilometre or more thick in places (approx.). Ask pupils why upland areas also grew their own glaciers (cold, snow). Pupils need only describe the extent: use 'north of a line from...'. Dates are approximate; check the latest consensus.

teach.heading: Freeze-thaw weathering
cycle: Water enters cracks in the rock
At night it freezes and expands by about 9%
It thaws by day and water goes deeper
Repeated cycles break off pieces, forming scree
teach.note: Demonstrate expansion with a sealed bottle of water in a freezer if possible (take care). The process needs temperatures that swing about freezing, as on upland slopes in winter. Scree collects beneath cliffs. Misconception: freeze-thaw only happens in glaciers; it is common in the UK uplands today.

teach.heading: Erosion processes

left.title: Plucking
points: Ice moves and pulls out chunks
Typical of back walls and valley steps

right.title: Abrasion
points: Rocks frozen in the ice scrape the surface
Like sandpaper, it smooths and scratches

teach.note: Draw a glacier in cross-section showing debris at its base. Add rotational movement in corries and basal sliding of ice on meltwater. Ice bulldozes loose material. Deposition occurs when ice melts and the load is dropped as unsorted till. Ask pupils: why does plucking leave a jagged surface while abrasion makes it smooth?

teach.heading: Skill: explain a process

model.problem: Explain how plucking and abrasion erode a glacial valley. (4 marks)
steps: Plucking: meltwater freezes to the valley sides and bed.
As the glacier moves it pulls pieces of rock away.
Abrasion: rocks embedded in the ice scrape the surface like sandpaper.
Result: the valley is widened, deepened and smoothed.
model.answer: In plucking, meltwater freezes onto the rock and as the glacier moves it pulls pieces away. In abrasion, rocks frozen into the base of the glacier scrape the rock like sandpaper. Together they widen and deepen the valley.

teach.note: I do. Pupils muddle the two processes. Plucking pulls; abrasion scrapes. Give a gesture for each.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which process involves ice pulling rock away as it moves?
check.why: Plucking: the ice freezes to the rock and pulls it away.

teach.note: Answer: B.

Stretch: Explain how glacial erosion processes work together to deepen a valley. (6 marks)
