lessons.unit: Unit 11: Glacial landscapes in the UK (AQA 3.1.3.4; OPTION: two of coasts, rivers, glaciers)
lessons.title: Glacial landforms of erosion and deposition: the Lake District
lessons.bigQuestion: What evidence of ice can we still see in today's landscape?
objectives: Explain erosional landforms: corries, arêtes, pyramidal peaks, truncated spurs, troughs, ribbon lakes and hanging valleys
Explain transport and deposition landforms: erratics, drumlins and moraines
Use the Lake District as a case study of a glaciated upland
successCriteria: All: name and sketch four glacial landforms
Most: explain how a corrie and an arête form
Some: explain the formation of glacial troughs, ribbon lakes and drumlins using a named upland
lessons.crossCurricular: Art: sketching landforms; Skills: OS map interpretation
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at landscapes shaped by immense forces over time

keywords.def: a bowl-shaped hollow high on a mountain, cut by ice
a sharp ridge between two corries
a spur cut off by a glacier
a long narrow lake in a glacial trough
an egg-shaped hill of till
a ridge of rock debris deposited by a glacier

starter: Say Bismillah. Name three processes of glacial erosion.
Describe the extent of the ice sheet in the UK.
Define 'freeze-thaw'.

teach.heading: Formation of a corrie

timeline.label: 1. Snow collects
timeline.text: Snow gathers in a hollow on a north- or east-facing slope; it turns to ice

timeline.label: 2. Freeze-thaw
timeline.text: Weathering loosens the back wall and nivation enlarges the hollow

timeline.label: 3. Rotation
timeline.text: The ice rotates, deepening the floor by abrasion; plucking steepens the back wall

timeline.label: 4. Retreat
timeline.text: When the ice melts, a steep back wall, a bowl and a rock lip remain

timeline.label: 5. Tarn
timeline.text: Water fills the hollow, forming a tarn such as Red Tarn on Helvellyn

teach.note: Corrie: also called cirque or cwm. Pupils should include freeze-thaw, plucking, abrasion and rotational slip. Stress that the hollow faces the direction that is shadier (in the UK the north-east). Ask: where is the rock lip, and why does it form? (Less erosion at the front where ice thins.) Link to Helvellyn in the Lake District: Red Tarn sits in a corrie and Striding Edge is an arête.

teach.heading: Erosional landforms

head: Landform
How it forms
Lake District / UK example
rows: Two corries erode back to back, leaving a knife-edge ridge
Three or more corries erode a mountain
A glacier deepens and straightens a river valley into a U-shape
Glacier cuts off the ends of spurs
Water fills an over-deepened part of the trough
A tributary valley left high above the trough; a waterfall forms

teach.note: Draw a cross-section of a glacial trough: U-shape, truncated spurs, hanging valleys on the sides, ribbon lake on the floor. Windermere is about 17 km long (approx.); Wastwater, England's deepest lake at about 79 m (approx.). Check examples against a good source before use; the principles are what AQA tests. Ask: why do trough sides appear steep? (Abrasion and plucking at the base and sides.)

teach.heading: Transport and deposition landforms

head: Landform
Description
Example
rows: Rocks carried a long way and dropped on different rock types
Egg-shaped hills of till; steeper end faces the ice, gently tapered end shows direction
Ridges of debris: lateral (sides), medial (centre), terminal (furthest advance)

teach.note: Ice transports material by bulldozing (pushing), by carrying debris on top, within and under the glacier. When the ice melts, the debris is dropped as till. Pupils must know the difference between a lateral and a terminal moraine. Norber erratics are boulders of Silurian rock sitting on limestone. The drumlin example is approximate: check with a local atlas or OS map.

teach.heading: Skill: explain formation of a landform

model.problem: Explain how an arête is formed. (3 marks)
steps: Two corries form on opposite sides of a mountain.
Plucking and abrasion erode their back walls so they cut backwards.
The land between them becomes a narrow, steep-sided ridge: the arête.
model.answer: Two corries form back to back on opposite sides of a mountain. Plucking and abrasion make the back walls retreat, which leaves a narrow, knife-edge ridge between them, called an arête.

teach.note: I do. Sketch it in two stages. The key is the idea of back-to-back erosion: pupils just say 'it is a ridge'.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: Which landform is made by deposition?
check.why: Drumlins are hills of till deposited by ice. The others are erosional.

teach.note: Answer: C.

practice: Draw and annotate a diagram of a glacial trough with truncated spurs, hanging valley and ribbon lake.
Complete a table of erosional and depositional landforms with a one-line formation explanation.
independent: Core: Name two features of a glacial trough. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain how a corrie is formed. (4 marks)
Stretch: Using a named UK glaciated upland, explain how its landforms were formed. (6 marks)
exit: Name a landform of erosion and a landform of deposition caused by ice.
Return to the big question: give one piece of evidence of ice in the landscape.
lessons.homework: Annotate a photo or OS map extract of the Helvellyn area or Snowdonia with at least five glacial features.
lessons.send: SEND: labelled landform cards to match with definitions. EAL: key terms with pictures. Stretch: explain why corries are mostly on north- and east-facing slopes.

lessons.unit: Unit 11: Glacial landscapes in the UK (AQA 3.1.3.4; OPTION: two of coasts, rivers, glaciers)
lessons.title: The Lake District: land use, conflict and managing tourism
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a beautiful landscape be shared between visitors, farmers and wildlife?
objectives: Describe economic activities in glaciated uplands: tourism, farming, forestry and quarrying
Discuss land-use conflicts and tensions between development and conservation
Explain impacts and management of tourism in the Lake District
successCriteria: All: name four land uses and one conflict
Most: explain impacts of tourism and how they are managed
Some: evaluate how effective management has been and reach a judgement
lessons.crossCurricular: Economics: opportunity cost; Citizenship: planning and local democracy
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship of land; fairness between visitors and local people

keywords.def: a place that attracts large numbers of visitors
a protected area with strict planning rules
disagreement between groups wanting different uses of the same land
wearing away of paths by walkers
tourism that can continue without harming the environment

starter: Say Bismillah. Name two glacial landforms of the Lake District.
Define 'ribbon lake'.
State one possible use of an upland area.

teach.heading: Economic activities in glaciated uplands

head: Activity
Why here
Problem
rows: Rough pasture; sheep such as Herdwicks
Thin soils, steep slopes and harsh weather; low incomes
Conifers grow on poor soils at altitude
Plantations change the landscape and wildlife
Hard rocks such as slate and granite
Noise, dust, lorries and scars on the landscape

teach.note: Ask pupils which activities are traditional and which are modern. In the Lake District, Honister is a working slate mine and Grizedale and Whinlatter are forests. Hill farming is part of the cultural landscape, and was recognised when the Lake District became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2017 (check wording). Keep the principle clear: glaciated uplands have steep slopes, thin soils and scenery.

teach.heading: A land-use conflict

left.title: Development and visitors
points: Second homes and shops serve visitors

right.title: Conservation and residents
points: Traffic jams and noise upset residents
Second homes push up house prices

teach.note: Ask pupils to role-play a public meeting: a hotel owner, a farmer, a walker, a conservation officer. Highlight that the Lake District has about 40,000 residents but welcomes many millions of visits each year (about 18 million, approx.; check the latest figures). Conflicts include second homes, jam-packed roads in summer and speedboats on Windermere (a 10 mph limit was introduced in 2005, approx.).

teach.heading: Case study: tourism in the Lake District National Park

head: Impact
Management
rows: Footpath erosion on popular fells such as Helvellyn
Path repairs by volunteers and groups (for example Fix the Fells); stone pitching and re-routing
Traffic and car parking at honeypots such as Ambleside and Keswick
Park-and-ride, buses and cycle routes; parking charges
Speed limit of 10 mph on Windermere
Planning rules and local housing policies
Education, wardens and sustainable tourism messages

teach.note: The Lake District became a national park in 1951 and covers about 2,362 square kilometres (approx.). The park authority balances conservation and recreation. Ask: which strategy do you think works best and why? Possible answers include education, since it changes behaviour, or path repairs, since they fix the damage directly. Check present policies; they change. Remind pupils that exam answers should name the place and a specific scheme.

teach.heading: Skill: assess management

model.problem: Assess the effectiveness of management of tourism in a named glaciated upland. (6 marks, outline)
steps: Problem with detail: footpath erosion on Helvellyn from large numbers of walkers.
Management: path repair projects with stone steps and re-routing.
Strength: it reduces erosion and keeps the paths usable.
Weakness: costly and relies on volunteers; visitor numbers keep rising.
Judgement: effective locally, but needs to be combined with limits on traffic and visitor education.
model.answer: In the Lake District, thousands of walkers cause footpath erosion on fells such as Helvellyn. Path repairs with stone steps reduce erosion and keep paths safe, but they are costly and depend on volunteers while visitor numbers keep growing. Overall the repairs are effective locally but work best alongside traffic management and education.

teach.note: I do. Show pupils to use named places and a clear judgement. Many answers stay general: 'visitors cause damage and rangers fix it'.

teach.heading: Hinge question

check.q: What is a honeypot site?
options: A site with a lot of wildlife
A place which attracts many visitors
check.why: A honeypot is a place that draws large numbers of visitors, such as Ambleside or Bowness-on-Windermere.

teach.note: Answer: B.

practice: Complete a table of land uses with one opportunity and one conflict each for the Lake District.
Role-play: write a 30-second statement for a farmer, a walker and a resident.
independent: Core: Give two economic activities found in glaciated uplands. (2 marks)
Extend: Explain one conflict between land uses in a glaciated upland. (3 marks)
Stretch: Assess the effectiveness of managing tourism in a named UK glaciated upland. (6 marks)
exit: Name one impact of tourism and one management strategy.
Return to the big question: give a reason for sharing and one challenge.
lessons.homework: Write a 150-word letter to the National Park Authority suggesting one way to reduce the impact of tourism.
lessons.send: SEND: pre-structured table for impacts and management. EAL: key terms with images. Stretch: compare management in the Lake District with another national park.

lessons.title: Cartographic skills: OS maps, grid references, scale, relief and gradient
lessons.bigQuestion: How do geographers read a map to find, measure and describe places?
objectives: Give four- and six-figure grid references
Measure distance using scale and describe direction
Describe relief and calculate gradient
successCriteria: All: give a four-figure reference and use a scale line
Most: give six-figure references and calculate distance
Some: calculate gradient and describe relief from contours
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: ratio, scale and gradient
lessons.smsc: Practical: using maps for travel (khalifah as responsible travellers)

keywords.def: a number code to find a place on a map; eastings first, then northings
the relationship between distance on the map and distance on the ground
a line joining places of equal height
how steep a slope is: vertical change divided by horizontal distance
the shape and height of the land

starter: Bismillah. What is the meaning of 1:50 000?
Name the eight compass points.
What does a contour line show?

teach.heading: Grid references
bullets: Four-figure reference gives a grid square.
Six-figure reference gives a point inside the square.

model.problem: Give a six-figure grid reference for a church in square 34 87, three tenths across and seven tenths up.
steps: Eastings: 34 then 3 tenths = 343.
Northings: 87 then 7 tenths = 877.
Write eastings first: 343877.

teach.note: Use the phrase 'along the corridor and up the stairs'. For a six-figure reference, divide each square into tenths by eye. A common error is reversing eastings and northings. Use an OS Explorer map for practice or the free online OS maps.

teach.heading: Scale and distance

check.q: On a 1:50 000 map, a straight-line distance measures 7.4 cm. What is the real distance?
check.why: 1 cm represents 0.5 km at 1:50 000, so 7.4 x 0.5 = 3.7 km. 7.4 km would mean 1 cm = 1 km; others are decimal-place errors.

teach.note: At 1:50 000, 1 cm = 500 m, so 2 cm = 1 km. Method: measure with a string for curved routes, then use the scale line. Worked: 7.4 cm x 0.5 km = 3.7 km. Misconception: forgetting to convert units. Ask pupils how scale 1:25 000 changes (1 cm = 250 m).

teach.heading: Direction and relief
bullets: Use eight compass points; bearings are measured clockwise from north.
Contour interval on OS 1:50 000 is usually 10 m.
teach.note: Ask pupils to describe a landscape using height, shape and slope: high ground in the north-west, a valley running south-east, steep slopes where contours are close. Relief descriptions need heights and place names. Caution: 'steep' needs evidence.

teach.heading: Gradient

model.problem: A path climbs from 120 m to 220 m over 2 km. Calculate the gradient.
steps: Vertical change = 220 - 120 = 100 m.
Convert horizontal distance: 2 km = 2000 m.
State as 1:20.

teach.note: Gradient = vertical rise / horizontal distance, in the same units. Show both ratio (1:20) and fraction. Example: a rise of 100 m over 2 km: 100 / 2000 = 1/20, gradient 1:20. A common error is mixing metres and kilometres.

teach.heading: Other map and image skills

head: Skill
Key points
rows: Simple outline, labels, title, key, north arrow
Mark heights from contours on a strip and join

teach.note: Sketch maps need a title, key, north arrow, frame and annotations. Photographs: describe foreground, middle ground and background, then annotate human and physical features. Link to fieldwork: field sketches record features. Ask pupils to draw a quick sketch map of a local route.

practice: Give the six-figure reference for a point 7 tenths across and 2 tenths up square 12 45. (1 mark)
A path rises 60 m over 1.5 km. Calculate the gradient. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Use scale to find the real length of a 9.2 cm route on a 1:50 000 map. (2 marks)
Extend: Describe the relief in a section of an OS map you are given. (3 marks)
Stretch: Explain how contours and gradient affect land use. (4 marks)
exit: Which comes first in a grid reference?
What is 1 cm on a 1:25 000 map in metres?
lessons.homework: Use an online OS map to give a six-figure reference for your local mosque or park and describe the relief.
lessons.send: SEND: enlarged maps and grid overlay. EAL: key words with images. Stretch: use trigonometry to calculate true slope.

lessons.title: Graphical skills: choosing and interpreting graphs and thematic maps
lessons.bigQuestion: Which graph or map shows the data best, and what does it tell us?
objectives: Choose a suitable graph or map for a data set
Read and describe bar, line, pie, histogram, scatter, pyramid, choropleth, isoline and flow-line maps
Describe patterns using data
successCriteria: All: name the right graph for simple data
Most: describe a population pyramid and a choropleth
Some: evaluate whether a graph is suitable and spot weaknesses
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: statistics and data; Science: graphs
lessons.smsc: Moral: presenting information honestly

keywords.def: a map using shades of one colour to show quantities in areas
a map with lines joining places of equal value, such as contours
a map using arrows or lines whose width shows the size of movement
a bar graph showing numbers or percentages by age and sex
a bar chart for continuous data with bars touching

starter: Bismillah. What is the difference between discrete and continuous data?
Name two types of graph.
What is a scatter graph used for?

teach.heading: Choosing the right graph

head: Graph or map
Best for
Example
rows: Distance from centre vs quality score

teach.note: Go through each choice with an example from geography. The key question: what is the data and what do I want to show? Misconception: pie charts for time. Check understanding with the question.

teach.heading: Population pyramids
bullets: Wide base: high birth rate and young population.
Narrow top: few elderly people, low life expectancy.
Narrow base and wide top: ageing population.

check.q: A population pyramid has a very wide base and a very narrow top. What does it suggest?
options: Low birth rate and long life expectancy
High birth rate and shorter life expectancy
check.why: A wide base means many children (high birth rate) and a narrow top means few older people (shorter life expectancy). Options A and D describe the opposite shape.

teach.note: Describe the shape, then evidence, then explain. For example, a pyramid for Nigeria has a wide base (about 40% under 15; approx., verify) while the UK has a more even shape with a bulge in middle age. Link to DTM stages in Y11.

teach.heading: Choropleth, isoline and flow-line maps

left.title: Choropleth
points: Colour shades show values per area

right.title: Isoline and flow-line
points: Isoline: lines join equal values (contours, isotherms)

teach.note: Use real examples: choropleth of GDP per person, isoline of rainfall or temperature, flow-line of migration. Teach reading a key. Misconception: shading in a choropleth shows the density of dots; it shows an average for the area. Remind that darker shading is usually higher value.

teach.heading: Describing a graph or map

model.problem: Describe the trend shown in a line graph of world urban population (30% in 1950, 55% in 2018). (2 marks)
steps: State the overall trend: it increases.
Quote data with units: from about 30% in 1950 to about 55% in 2018.
Add detail: the rise is steady across the period.
Do not explain causes: the question says describe.
model.answer: Urban population increased steadily from approx. 30% to approx. 55%.

teach.note: Teach the structure: overall trend, specific data with units, anomalies. Avoid explaining unless asked. Model with a line graph of urban population: 'increases from about 30% in 1950 to about 55% in 2018, rising most quickly after 1990.'

practice: State the best graph for showing the percentage of energy from each source in the UK. (1 mark)
Describe the pyramid shape of a country with a high birth rate. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Describe the pattern shown on a choropleth map of life expectancy. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain why a flow-line map is suitable to show migration. (2 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate how suitable a pie chart is for showing change over time. (4 marks)
exit: Give one use for a scatter graph.
What does a wide base on a pyramid show?
lessons.homework: Find one graph or map in a news article and write a description and evaluation of it.
lessons.send: SEND: graph templates. EAL: labelled diagrams. Stretch: draw a pyramid from census data for your local area.

lessons.title: Numerical and statistical skills: averages, spread, percentage change and cumulative frequency
lessons.bigQuestion: How do geographers use numbers to be accurate, and how can data mislead?
objectives: Calculate mean, median, mode, range, interquartile range and percentage change
Use cumulative frequency and percentiles
Identify misleading presentation of data
successCriteria: All: calculate mean, median and range
Most: find the interquartile range and percentage change
Some: use cumulative frequency and evaluate a misleading graph
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: statistics, ratio, proportion
lessons.smsc: Moral: honesty and fairness in presenting data (sidq)

keywords.def: the sum of all values divided by the number of values
the middle value in ordered data
upper quartile minus lower quartile: the spread of the middle 50%
a running total of frequencies
the change divided by the original value, multiplied by 100
a value far from the others

starter: Bismillah. Find the median of 4, 7, 9, 12, 13.
What does range show?
Convert 3/20 into a percentage.

teach.heading: Averages and spread

model.problem: Find the median, quartiles and interquartile range of: 7, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 23, 29.
steps: Median is the 6th value of 11: 15.
Lower half: 7, 9, 11, 12, 14. Lower quartile = 11.
Upper half: 16, 18, 20, 23, 29. Upper quartile = 20.
model.answer: Median 15, quartiles 11 and 20, IQR 9.

teach.note: Data: pebble lengths in cm: 7, 9, 11, 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 20, 23, 29 (n = 11). Sum 174, mean 15.8 (to 1 d.p.), median 15, range 22. Lower quartile = median of 7, 9, 11, 12, 14 = 11. Upper quartile = median of 16, 18, 20, 23, 29 = 20. IQR = 20 - 11 = 9. The outlier 29 pulls the mean above the median.

teach.heading: Percentage change

check.q: A city grows from 2.4 million to 3.0 million people. What is the percentage increase?
check.why: Change is 0.6 million; 0.6 / 2.4 = 0.25 = 25%. 20% divides by the new value; 60% is the raw difference of 0.6 as a percentage; 0.6% is incorrect.

teach.note: Method: (new - old) / old x 100. Example: city population 2.4 million to 3.0 million. Change 0.6, 0.6 / 2.4 = 0.25, so 25% increase. Decrease: negative. Common error: dividing by the new figure. Ask pupils to calculate a decrease from 50 to 40 (20% decrease).

teach.heading: Cumulative frequency and percentiles
bullets: Add each frequency to the running total.
Plot against the upper class boundary.
Read the median at half the total; quartiles at 25% and 75%.
cycle: Plot the points (upper boundary, cumulative total)
teach.note: Use a quick example: 40 pupils' journey times; the median is at the 20th value (20/40), the lower quartile at 10, the upper quartile at 30. Percentile: the value below which a given percentage falls, so the 90th percentile means 90% fall below. Ask: what use is this for pebble sizes or river data? (Compare sites.)

teach.heading: Number, ratio and area
teach.note: Show how ratio and proportion appear: 'a ratio of 3:1 urban to rural means 75% urban'. Area: a map square at 1:50 000 is 1 km x 1 km = 1 km2. Frequency tables and data sheets need clear headings, units and space for the collectors' initials. Give pupils a data sheet design task.

teach.heading: Misleading data

misconception.wrong: A bar chart that starts its y-axis at 90 shows a small difference accurately.
misconception.right: A truncated axis exaggerates differences; always check the scale, the sample size and the source.

teach.note: Present a graph with a truncated y-axis, an uneven time scale or an unfair sample. Ask: who could be misled and how? Link to honesty and amanah. Remind pupils that exam questions ask to evaluate data.

practice: Calculate the mean of 6, 8, 10, 12, 14. (1 mark)
A town's population falls from 50 000 to 45 000. Calculate the percentage decrease. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Calculate the median and range for the data set 3, 5, 8, 9, 14, 20, 22. (3 marks)
Extend: Calculate the interquartile range of the same data. (3 marks)
Stretch: Explain two ways a graph of river data could be misleading. (4 marks)
exit: What is the formula for percentage change?
Which average is least affected by an outlier?
lessons.homework: Use rainfall data for a place of your choice for twelve months: calculate the mean, median and range.
lessons.send: SEND: step-by-step calculation frame. EAL: key terms with worked numeric examples. Stretch: draw a cumulative frequency curve and estimate the 90th percentile.

lessons.title: Using data, GIS and satellite images; enquiry, argument and geographical writing
lessons.bigQuestion: How do geographers use different data and write convincing answers?
objectives: Distinguish qualitative and quantitative data and use GIS and satellite imagery
Frame questions and build evidenced conclusions
Write clearly for different audiences with accurate SPaG
successCriteria: All: classify data as qualitative or quantitative
Most: interpret a satellite image or GIS layer
Some: write an evidence-based argument with correct SPaG
lessons.crossCurricular: English: writing and argument; Computing: data and mapping tools
lessons.smsc: Moral: speaking with truth and clarity (sidq)

keywords.def: descriptive data such as opinions, sketches and photos
numerical data such as counts and measurements
Geographical Information System: software that layers maps and data
a picture of the Earth taken from space
facts or data used to support a point

starter: Bismillah. Give one quantitative and one qualitative example from a river study.
What does GIS stand for?
What does 'justify' mean?

teach.heading: Qualitative and quantitative data
teach.note: Distinguish between them using fieldwork examples. Ask pupils to place each example in the table and say how each could be used together: interviews explain why numbers look as they do. Misconception: qualitative is 'worse'; both are useful. Strengths: quantitative can be graphed; qualitative explains experiences.

teach.heading: GIS and satellite imagery
bullets: GIS stacks map layers: roads, flood zones, population.
Satellite images show land use, settlement growth and hazards.
Compare images from different years to see change.

check.q: What is the main advantage of GIS for a geographer?
options: It collects data in the field
It layers different data sets on maps to compare patterns
check.why: GIS combines layers so patterns can be compared, for example flood zones and housing. It does not replace fieldwork.

teach.note: Show a satellite image of a city (for example Lagos lagoon) and compare with an older one. Ask pupils to identify land use. Model how to use GIS: choose layers, switch on and compare. Useful free tools: Google Earth, ArcGIS Online, NASA Worldview. Limitation: resolution, cloud, date.

teach.heading: Framing questions and building arguments

model.problem: Write a PEEL paragraph: 'Rapid growth creates problems in Lagos.'
steps: Point: rapid growth creates challenges for housing.
Evidence: informal settlements like Makoko hold large numbers of people without proper services.
Explanation: this happens because migration is faster than the supply of homes and sewers.
Link: so growth must be matched by planning to improve quality of life.
model.answer: A paragraph using point, evidence, explanation and link.

teach.note: Model an argument: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link. Show how to move from a descriptive to an evaluative question. Ask pupils to turn 'Describe Lagos' into 'To what extent does Lagos offer opportunity?' Stress that conclusions must follow from evidence.

teach.heading: Writing for different audiences
teach.note: Show two versions: a formal exam answer and a short summary for a local council. Teach exam answers: clear, precise, correct terminology, use connectives like 'therefore', 'as a result'. SPaG: capital letters for named places, consistent tense, accurate spelling of key words. Ask pupils to improve a weak sentence.

practice: Classify each as qualitative or quantitative: a questionnaire score, a photograph, a traffic count, an interview opinion. (2 marks)
Explain one limitation of satellite images. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Describe how GIS could be used to plan a flood defence scheme. (3 marks)
Extend: Write a PEEL paragraph on why informal settlements grow. (4 marks)
Stretch: Rewrite your paragraph for a council leaflet. Explain how and why it differs. (4 marks)
exit: Give one example of qualitative data.
What does PEEL stand for?
lessons.homework: Write a short geographical argument (about 120 words) on a local issue, using one piece of quantitative evidence.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters and a PEEL frame. EAL: word bank and bilingual glossary. Stretch: write for two audiences and compare tone.

lessons.title: Global urban change, urbanisation and megacities
lessons.bigQuestion: Why are more people living in cities than ever before, and where is it happening fastest?
objectives: Describe global patterns of urban change since 1950
Explain how migration and natural increase drive urbanisation
Explain the rise of megacities and compare urban trends in HICs and LICs/NEEs
successCriteria: All: define urbanisation and give two causes
Most: explain push and pull factors and natural increase, with figures
Some: compare urban trends in HICs with LICs/NEEs and explain the differences
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: percentages and reading line graphs
lessons.smsc: Social: community and neighbourliness (jiwar) when large numbers of people live close together

keywords.def: the increase in the proportion of a country's population living in towns and cities
a city with a population of over 10 million people
the movement of people from the countryside to cities
births minus deaths; the growth of a population without migration
something that encourages people to leave a place
something that attracts people to a place

starter: Bismillah. Define 'population density' and name one densely populated country.
What is the difference between a rural and an urban settlement?
Which continent has the largest population? Estimate its share of the world total.

teach.heading: The world has gone urban

timeline.text: About 30% of the world lived in cities (approx.)
For the first time, over half of people were urban
About 55% urban, around 4.2 billion people (approx.)
Projected about 68% urban, with most growth in Asia and Africa

teach.note: Say that the UN (World Urbanization Prospects) estimates 2007 was the first year when more than half of people lived in cities. Ask pupils to predict the 2050 figure before revealing it. Stress that figures are approximate and projections. Ask: which part of the world was most urban in 1950 and which is changing fastest now? (Africa and Asia.)

teach.heading: Why do cities grow? Two drivers
bullets: Migration: people move from rural areas to cities.
Natural increase: young migrants have children, so births exceed deaths.
Both together make growth rapid and self-reinforcing.
cycle: Young adults migrate to the city for work
They have children in the city
teach.note: Introduce the cycle as a feedback loop. Common misconception: pupils think urbanisation is only migration. Point out that in many LIC cities natural increase now accounts for a large share of growth. Ask: why do migrants tend to be young adults? (They seek work and are able to move.)

teach.heading: Push and pull factors

left.title: Push (rural area)
points: Farm jobs lost as farming is mechanised

right.title: Pull (city)
points: Hope of a better quality of life

teach.note: Ask pupils to sort each point into economic, social or environmental. Link to places they know of: drought and mechanisation of farming push people out; jobs, schools and clinics pull them in. Remind pupils that pull factors can be perceived, not real: migrants can end up in a slum, not the job they expected.

teach.heading: Megacities: where are they?
bullets: Megacity means 10 million or more people.
In 1950 there were two; by 2018 about 33 (UN).
Most new megacities are in Asia, Africa and Latin America.
teach.note: Use the table; say figures are approximate (UN 2018, rounded) and teacher should confirm the latest edition. Ask: which cities are in HICs? (Tokyo, and Osaka.) Which are in LICs/NEEs? Most of the rest. Note the table is about city size, not wealth.

teach.heading: HICs and LICs/NEEs: different trends
bullets: HICs urbanised in the 1800s and 1900s with industry.
LICs/NEEs are urbanising now, far more quickly.
In HICs some people now leave cities: counterurbanisation.

model.problem: Explain why urban growth is faster in Nigeria than in the UK. (4 marks)
steps: Point: Nigeria is at an earlier stage of urbanisation (about half urban, approx.).
Evidence: millions of rural people migrate to Lagos for jobs in services and industry.
Point: Nigeria has high natural increase.
Evidence: young migrants have large families, so births exceed deaths.
Contrast: the UK urbanised in the 1800s, so few rural people are left to migrate.
model.answer: Nigeria is still urbanising through rural-urban migration and high natural increase; the UK completed most of this change over a century ago.

teach.note: Check understanding with the model. The UK is about 83% urban (approx., World Bank) and growing slowly; Nigeria roughly half urban (approx.) and growing quickly. Misconception: 'HIC cities have stopped growing'. Many, like London, still grow, mainly by migration and natural increase, but the pace is much slower.

teach.heading: Check your understanding

check.q: Which is a PUSH factor for rural-urban migration?
options: A hospital opening in the city
A new factory in the city
check.why: Drought and poor farmland push people away from the countryside. The other three are pull factors: they attract people to the city.

teach.note: Hinge on whiteboards. Answer is B. A is natural increase; C describes counterurbanisation; D is a pull factor but wrong choice as it would be a push factor for a rural area. Look for pupils choosing D.

practice: Describe the trend shown for the proportion of the world living in cities between 1950 and 2018. Use figures. (2 marks)
State two reasons why megacities are growing fastest in Asia and Africa.
independent: Core: Explain two push and two pull factors that cause rural-urban migration. (4 marks)
Extend: Explain how natural increase adds to urban growth. (3 marks)
Stretch: Compare urban trends in a HIC and a LIC/NEE. Use the words 'counterurbanisation' and 'rural-urban migration'. (6 marks)
exit: Define urbanisation in your own words.
Give one reason why Delhi has grown into a megacity.
lessons.homework: Research the current population of one megacity from the table and write three sentences on why it grew.
lessons.send: SEND: sort push and pull cards before writing. EAL: word bank with pictures. Stretch: draw an urban growth graph from UN data and describe anomalies.

lessons.title: Lagos: a major city in an NEE: location, growth and opportunities
lessons.bigQuestion: Why has Lagos grown so fast, and what does it offer the people who move there?
objectives: Locate Lagos and explain its importance nationally and internationally
Explain the causes of its rapid growth
Assess the economic and social opportunities it offers
successCriteria: All: locate Lagos and state two reasons for growth
Most: explain how migration and natural increase led to growth, with data
Some: assess how far opportunities are shared by all residents
lessons.crossCurricular: History: colonial trade and the Nigerian economy
lessons.smsc: Social: economic opportunity and responsibility to the poor (zakat and sadaqah as a principle of sharing wealth)

keywords.def: newly emerging economy: a country with rapid economic growth, such as Nigeria
jobs with no contracts, tax or regulation, such as street trading
a coastal place where goods are loaded and unloaded from ships
regulated jobs with contracts and tax, such as banking

starter: Bismillah. Name two of the megacities from last lesson.
Explain one push factor and one pull factor.
What does NEE stand for?

teach.heading: Where is Lagos?
bullets: South-west Nigeria, on the Gulf of Guinea coast.
Built around the Lagos Lagoon and islands.
Nigeria's biggest city and former capital (capital moved to Abuja in 1991).

head: Fact
Detail
rows: Nigeria, West Africa, Gulf of Guinea coast
Lagoon, islands and mainland; major port
Largest city in Nigeria; capital until 1991

teach.note: Use an atlas. Ask pupils to describe location at three scales: Africa, West Africa, Nigeria. Note Lagos is a port with the largest container terminals in the country (Apapa and Tin Can). The population is approx. 15 million+ depending on boundary definition (city and metro estimates vary widely); flag the figure for the teacher to update. Check before use: Blue Line light rail opens and Dangote refinery starts production (verify)

teach.heading: A city that grew very fast

timeline.text: Population around 0.3 million (approx.)
Capital moves to Abuja, but Lagos keeps its economic role
BRT-Lite bus system opens, one of Africa's first
Around 13 to 15 million people (approx., definitions vary)
Blue Line light rail opens and Dangote refinery starts production

teach.note: Use the timeline; all figures approx. Ask pupils to calculate growth: from about 0.3 million to over 14 million. Draw out that migration brought young adults and natural increase followed. Ask: what is the 'multiplier' effect of a large port and oil money? (Jobs, services, further migration.) Be explicit that Lagos is not the world's largest city; it is the fastest-growing example in the NEE category.

teach.heading: Why did it grow?
bullets: Port trade: oil and goods exports and imports.
Migration from rural areas of Nigeria and neighbouring countries.
High natural increase among young migrants.
Industry, banking, media and the Nollywood film industry.

check.q: Which best explains why Lagos continues to attract migrants?
options: Government orders people to move there
It offers jobs in port, industry and services
Rural areas of Nigeria have no people left
It is the capital city of Nigeria
check.why: Jobs and services are the main pull. Lagos has not been the capital since 1991, and rural areas still hold millions of people, so the other options are false.

teach.note: Prompt pupils to build a causal chain rather than list factors. Misconception: 'Lagos grows because the government told people to move.' Actually people moved for opportunity: push factors (poverty, conflict in the north-east, falling farm incomes) and pull factors (jobs, services). The Nollywood film industry is among the largest in the world by volume (verify exact ranking).

teach.heading: Opportunities in Lagos

head: Type
Examples in Lagos
rows: Banking, port, Lekki Free Zone, Dangote refinery (opened 2023-24), Nollywood
Street trading, transport, recycling, small workshops
Universities such as the University of Lagos, more schools than rural areas
More hospitals and clinics than in the countryside
Better chance of electricity and mobile phone access

teach.note: Table gives sorting categories. Ask pupils to rank which are most important for a young migrant. Draw out that many jobs are informal (street trading, transport, recycling) and give income but not security. The Lekki Free Zone and Dangote refinery are examples of large-scale formal investment (state dates as approx.). Emphasise equity: opportunities are not equally shared.

teach.heading: Model: a 6-mark answer plan

model.problem: Assess how far Lagos offers opportunities for people living there. (6 marks)
steps: Opportunity: formal jobs in port, banking and manufacturing pay more than farming.
Evidence: Dangote refinery and Lekki Free Zone attract investment.
Opportunity: education and health services are better than in rural Nigeria.
Limit: many people work informally with low and uncertain income.
Limit: opportunities are often not available to people living in slums.
Judgement: Lagos offers genuine opportunity, but mainly to those with skills, capital or contacts.
model.answer: Opportunities are real but unevenly shared, so they are limited for the poorest.

teach.note: Show how to structure evidence, explanation and judgement. Remind pupils that 'assess' needs a judgement of importance or extent. Ask them to underline the judgement phrase.

practice: Describe the location of Lagos using two of: coast, lagoon, port, Nigeria, Gulf of Guinea. (2 marks)
Explain one economic and one social opportunity in Lagos. (4 marks)
independent: Core: Explain why Lagos has grown so rapidly. (4 marks)
Extend: Suggest why informal work is an opportunity and a problem for migrants. (3 marks)
Stretch: Assess how far Lagos offers opportunities for people living there. (6 marks)
exit: Give two reasons Lagos has grown.
Name one formal and one informal job in Lagos.
lessons.homework: Find a recent news article about Lagos, then write 100 words saying whether it shows an opportunity or a challenge.
lessons.send: SEND: causal chain scaffold. EAL: translate keywords. Stretch: calculate growth from 0.3 to about 14 million as a multiple.

lessons.title: Lagos: challenges of rapid growth, slums and services
lessons.bigQuestion: What problems does rapid urban growth create, and who suffers most?
objectives: Describe the challenges of rapid growth in Lagos
Explain why slums and informal settlements form
Evaluate the impact on quality of life
successCriteria: All: name three challenges in Lagos
Most: explain how each challenge arises from rapid growth
Some: evaluate which challenge is most serious and for whom
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: sanitation, waste and disease
lessons.smsc: Moral: dignity (karamah) of every person, including residents of informal settlements

keywords.def: an area of makeshift housing built without legal permission, also called a slum or informal settlement
too much traffic making travel slow
housing built without planning permission, often lacking services

starter: Bismillah. State two opportunities in Lagos.
Define 'informal economy'.
What is the difference between the formal and informal economy?

teach.heading: Housing: slums and informal settlements
bullets: Housing cannot be built as fast as the city grows.
Many people live in informal settlements like Makoko.
Houses are built from wood and scrap on stilts or any free land.

left.title: Why slums form
points: Migration is faster than house building
Formal housing is too expensive for low earners
Land is scarce on islands and lagoon edges

right.title: Life in a slum
points: Risk of flood, fire and eviction

teach.note: Makoko, on the Lagos Lagoon, is a floating community of stilted homes; population estimates vary widely (approx. 100,000 or more; verify). Residents are fishers and traders. Stress dignity: slums are communities with people's work and social life. Discuss the 2012 and 2017 eviction threats (state as flagged). Ask: why can't poor people simply rent formal housing? (Cost, rules, shortage.)

teach.heading: Services, jobs and the environment

head: Challenge
What happens in Lagos
Why
rows: Many homes lack piped water and sewers
Infrastructure cannot keep up with growth
Many work informally, with low pay and no security
Many cars, few roads, limited public transport
Air pollution from traffic and generators
Rubbish in drains and lagoons; large landfills

teach.note: Use the table to sort challenges. Ask pupils to pair a cause with each effect. Emphasise the link between lack of clean water and disease (cholera). Waste: the Olusosun landfill is among the largest in Africa (verify details). Pollution: traffic and generators produce air pollution because grid electricity is unreliable.

teach.heading: Traffic and pollution
bullets: Travel across the city can take hours at peak times.
Diesel generators and old vehicles pollute the air.
Flooding is worse where drains are blocked with rubbish.

check.q: Which statement best explains why slums form in Lagos?
options: Planners want people to live there
Migration is faster than affordable housing can be built
Lagos has no space for any housing
check.why: Slums form because housing supply does not keep pace with migration. Other statements are not supported by evidence.

teach.note: Link to quality of life: long commutes cost money and time. Note the Lagos BRT and Blue Line rail (2023) are responses; they appear in the next lesson. Ask for one effect on health and one on the economy.

teach.heading: Model: explain a challenge

model.problem: Explain how rapid growth can lead to health problems in Lagos slums. (4 marks)
steps: Rapid migration means more people than houses and services.
Many informal homes have no piped water or sewers.
Waste and dirty water spread infectious diseases such as cholera.
Overcrowding helps diseases spread and healthcare is hard to reach.
model.answer: Rapid growth outpaces services, so poor sanitation and crowding spread disease.

teach.note: Walk through the chain: cause, effect, consequence. Say aloud the connective words. Ask pupils to apply the same chain to waste.

practice: Describe two features of the informal settlement of Makoko. (2 marks)
Explain why unemployment and underemployment occur in Lagos. (3 marks)
independent: Core: Explain two challenges caused by rapid urban growth in Lagos. (4 marks)
Extend: Suggest why slum residents are often reluctant to move even if housing is poor. (3 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate which challenge in Lagos is the most serious. (6 marks)
exit: Name three challenges in Lagos.
Why do slums form?
lessons.homework: Draw a labelled sketch of a squatter settlement and annotate three challenges.
lessons.send: SEND: cause-effect cards. EAL: key vocabulary sheet. Stretch: compare Lagos and Mumbai's slum problems.

lessons.title: Urban planning for the urban poor: Rio de Janeiro's Favela Bairro
lessons.bigQuestion: Can planning make life better for people living in informal settlements?
objectives: Describe the Favela Bairro project in Rio de Janeiro
Explain how it improved quality of life
Evaluate its strengths and limitations as urban planning
successCriteria: All: name two things Favela Bairro changed
Most: explain why upgrading is better than demolition
Some: evaluate how successful the project was
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Brazil's urban development and Portuguese colonial legacy
lessons.smsc: Moral: justice and care for the poor (ihsan)

keywords.def: a Brazilian informal settlement or slum, often on steep hillsides
a project where residents build or improve their own homes with materials or training from authorities
improving services and housing in an existing settlement rather than demolishing it
meeting present needs without harming future generations

starter: Bismillah. Define squatter settlement.
Name two challenges in Lagos.
What is a sustainable city?

teach.heading: Rio and its favelas
bullets: Rio de Janeiro is Brazil's second-largest city.
Many favelas grew on steep hillsides near jobs.
Rocinha is among the largest, with about 70,000 people officially (2010 census).

head: Fact
Detail
rows: Rio de Janeiro, south-east Brazil, on the Atlantic coast
Steep hillsides close to jobs and wealthy districts
No sewers, narrow paths, poor water, no land titles

teach.note: Show the contrast of favelas beside wealthy neighbourhoods. State that census undercounts exist and unofficial estimates are higher. Ask: why would people build on steep hillsides? (Land is unclaimed and near jobs.) Avoid stereotypes: favelas contain businesses, schools and strong communities. Check before use: Rocinha is among the largest, with about 70,000 people officially (2010 census; verify). | About 70,000 official residents (2010 census; verify)

teach.heading: What was Favela Bairro?
bullets: Launched in 1994 by Rio's city government.
Upgraded existing favelas instead of demolishing them.
Aimed to turn favelas into normal neighbourhoods ('bairros').

timeline.label: 1980s
timeline.text: Evictions and demolition were common
Favela Bairro begins: pave, drain, light and connect

timeline.label: 1990s
timeline.text: Water, sewers, electricity, paved streets and community centres built
Morar Carioca plans to extend upgrading
Cable car links Complexo do Alemao to the train network

teach.note: Dates are approximate; the main programme began in the mid-1990s and was followed by Morar Carioca (2010). Ask: why is upgrading cheaper and more acceptable than demolition? (Keeps community, jobs, and cost lower.) Mention the Complexo do Alemao cable car (2011) as a related transport project.

teach.heading: What changed?

head: Improvement
Effect on residents
rows: Easier access for ambulances and buses
Safer, healthier homes and study at night
Security against eviction; houses can be improved

teach.note: Ask pupils to rank improvements by importance for health. Point out residents were consulted in some projects, and legal ownership (title) gave security. Link to sustainable development: the project is social and economic, but not environmentally complete.

teach.heading: Strengths and limits

right.title: Limitations
points: Rising costs may force poorer people out

teach.note: Prompt pupils to judge, not describe. Criticisms: not all favelas included; crime and drug gangs remain; maintenance of services is weak; some residents moved out as property values rose. State that evaluations differ.

teach.heading: Check your understanding

check.q: Why did planners choose to upgrade favelas rather than demolish them?
options: It is cheaper and keeps communities and jobs in place
check.why: Upgrading is cheaper and keeps social networks and work close. Demolition forces people to move and often creates new slums.

teach.note: Use the check to ensure pupils see why upgrading helps. Answer B; watch for pupils choosing A because they assume all slum change harms people.

teach.heading: Model: evaluating a scheme

model.problem: Evaluate the success of Favela Bairro. (6 marks)
steps: Strength: sewers, water and paved streets improved health and access.
Strength: legal titles gave people security and encouraged home improvement.
Limit: only some favelas were upgraded, and services were not always maintained.
Limit: crime remained and rising property values could push poorer people out.
Judgement: it was largely successful in improving daily life, but not complete or permanent.
model.answer: Judgement: mostly successful for those included, because services improved, but limited by scale and upkeep.

teach.note: Model the judgement sentence on the board. Pupils then copy the structure for the independent task: strength, limit, overall verdict with a reason.

practice: Describe two ways Favela Bairro improved the lives of favela residents. (2 marks)
Explain why legal ownership of homes matters. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain how urban planning in Rio has improved life for the urban poor. (4 marks)
Extend: Suggest one reason the project did not solve every problem. (2 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate the success of Favela Bairro. (6 marks)
exit: Give two features of Favela Bairro.
What does 'upgrading' mean?
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word speech from a favela resident explaining what changed after the scheme.
lessons.send: SEND: matching cards. EAL: glossary. Stretch: compare with self-help schemes such as Dharavi in Mumbai.

lessons.title: A major UK city: London's migration, opportunities, inequalities and sprawl
lessons.bigQuestion: What makes London both a city of opportunity and a city of inequality?
objectives: Locate London and explain its national and global importance
Explain the effects of migration on its character
Describe inequalities and urban sprawl, including commuter settlements
successCriteria: All: describe London's location and one effect of migration
Most: explain the opportunities and inequalities
Some: assess how sprawl and commuter settlements affect land and people
lessons.crossCurricular: Citizenship: communities and diversity
lessons.smsc: Social: respecting neighbours and different traditions (adab)

keywords.def: unequal distribution of wealth, income, health or opportunities
unplanned outward growth of a city into surrounding countryside
a town or village where many residents travel to work in the nearby city
land around a city where building is restricted
having people of many cultures and ethnic groups

starter: Bismillah. Define urban sprawl.
Name one challenge of urban growth in Lagos.
What is a commuter?

teach.heading: Why London matters
bullets: On the River Thames in south-east England.
Capital, financial centre, port and global city.

head: Role
Evidence
rows: The City and Canary Wharf; many global banks
Heathrow, rail termini, the Elizabeth line (opened 2022)
Parliament and national institutions in Westminster

teach.note: Use the figure 8.8 million (2021 Census, England and Wales); about 40% of London residents were born outside the UK (2021 Census approx.). Ask pupils for national and international roles. Mention Heathrow, the City, and universities. Verify the latest data if repeating the lesson.

teach.heading: Migration shapes London
bullets: International migration since Roman times; large waves after 1945.
Roughly 40% of residents were born abroad (2021, approx.).
Migrants bring skills, businesses and cultural diversity.

left.title: Opportunities
points: Workers for NHS, transport and construction

right.title: Challenges
points: Pressure on schools and GP services
Segregation or language barriers in some areas
Some migrants in low-paid insecure jobs

teach.note: Teach neutrally: describe effects, not people. Opportunities include filling skills gaps (NHS, construction), new businesses and food and festivals. Challenges include pressure on housing and school places and language barriers. Ask pupils to avoid generalisations. Draw out national migration: young graduates move to London for work.

teach.heading: Inequality within London

model.problem: Describe the inequality shown by a choropleth of deprivation in London. (2 marks)
steps: State the pattern: the most deprived areas are concentrated in inner east and some outer boroughs.
Support with data: name a borough and its rank or percentage.
Add contrast: wealthier areas lie mainly in the west and south-west and outer edges.
model.answer: Deprivation is clustered in parts of east London, with wealth in west and south-west; always quote a place and data.

teach.note: Use the model to practise data language. Say that boroughs differ sharply in income, housing and life expectancy; for example some inner east London boroughs such as Tower Hamlets have among the highest child poverty rates in the UK while others nearby are wealthy (verify current figures with the Indices of Multiple Deprivation or London Datastore). Ask: why does inequality persist? (Housing costs, wages, education, inherited wealth.)

teach.heading: Sprawl and commuter settlements
bullets: London grew outwards in the 1900s as railways and cars arrived.
The green belt (1947 planning law) limits outward growth.
Commuter towns in Kent, Essex and Hertfordshire house workers.

check.q: Which best defines a commuter settlement?
options: A settlement where many residents travel to a nearby city for work
A settlement in the green belt that bans homes
check.why: Commuter settlements house people whose jobs are in the city. The other options are inaccurate.

teach.note: Ask: what are the benefits of the green belt? (Protects farmland, recreation, limits sprawl.) Drawbacks: pushes development to beyond-green-belt commuter towns, raises house prices. Check understanding with the whiteboard question.

teach.heading: Putting it together

timeline.label: 1800s
timeline.text: Railways and industry expand London rapidly

timeline.label: 1930s
timeline.text: Suburbs spread, growth of commuter belts
Town and Country Planning Act and the green belt idea
Olympic Games and East London regeneration
Elizabeth line opens, linking commuter towns to the centre

teach.note: Recap with the three-word summary: 'diverse, unequal, spreading'. Ask pupils to connect: inequality leads to some commuters being wealthy and some low earners living in expensive inner areas. Prepare for next lesson on regeneration.

practice: Describe two ways migration has changed London. (2 marks)
Explain one reason inequality exists between London boroughs. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Explain how migration has created opportunities and challenges in London. (4 marks)
Extend: Describe the effects of urban sprawl on the countryside. (3 marks)
Stretch: Assess how far London is a city of opportunity for all of its residents. (6 marks)
exit: Define commuter settlement.
State two opportunities from migration.
lessons.homework: Use an online map to compare two London boroughs on house price, income or deprivation, and write a paragraph on what you find.
lessons.send: SEND: borough fact cards. EAL: key vocabulary. Stretch: link inequality with transport access (PTAL).

lessons.title: Regeneration and sustainable urban living: Stratford and the Olympic Park
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a city repair neglected land, and how can it be made sustainable?
objectives: Explain why regeneration was needed in East London and describe the Olympic Park project
Evaluate its impact on people, economy and environment
Describe sustainable urban living and traffic management strategies
successCriteria: All: describe one change from the Olympic regeneration
Most: explain reasons for regeneration and two benefits
Some: evaluate success and compare traffic management strategies
lessons.crossCurricular: Design and Technology: sustainable design; PE: Olympic legacy
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship (khalifah) of the Earth; avoiding waste (Qur'an 7:31 forbids wastefulness)

keywords.def: investment to improve a run-down area by bringing in jobs, homes and services
land that has been built on before and is available for reuse
the long-term effects of an event after it has ended
a city that meets its needs without harming future generations
a fee to drive in a central city zone to reduce traffic

starter: Bismillah. Define urban sprawl.
What is a brownfield site?
Name two problems of congestion.

teach.heading: Why regenerate Stratford?
bullets: Lower Lea Valley in East London had old industry and derelict land.
High unemployment and deprivation compared with London average.
Polluted land and poor transport links.
cycle: Clean land, build venues and transport
teach.note: Show a before picture if available. State that the area was previously heavily industrial, with contaminated land. The 2012 Olympics gave a deadline and funding. The public sector funding for the Games was around £9 billion (approx.; verify). Ask pupils: why choose a brownfield site rather than green belt? (Reuse, stops sprawl.)

teach.heading: What was built?

head: Change
Type of benefit
rows: Stratford International, Jubilee line and DLR upgrades
Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, wetlands, cleaned river
Aquatics Centre and Velodrome open to the public

teach.note: Ask pupils to categorise by economic, social, environmental. Mention East Village (the athletes' village) was converted into about 2,800 homes (approx.; verify), including affordable housing, and Westfield Stratford City opened 2011. Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park reopened in 2013 with a mix of venues, parkland and wetland.

teach.heading: Success or failure?

left.title: Successes
points: Sports venues and parkland for all

right.title: Criticisms
points: Local people did not always get the jobs

teach.note: Encourage balanced evaluation. Evidence of success: new jobs, new homes, regenerated land. Criticisms: rising house prices, affordable homes shortage, jobs often went to people from outside the area, and construction cost overruns. Avoid claiming figures you cannot verify. Link to the 6-mark pattern.

teach.heading: Sustainable urban living
bullets: Water and energy conservation: smart meters, green roofs.
More green space and urban farming.
Waste reduction and recycling in homes and businesses.

check.q: Which is an example of sustainable urban living?
options: Recycling and green roofs on new housing
check.why: Recycling and green roofs reduce waste and energy use. The other options increase resource use or damage land.

teach.note: BedZED (Beddington Zero Energy Development) in Sutton, London was an early eco-housing scheme. Mention that sustainability has three aspects: economic, social, environmental. Ask: how can a household help? Link to Islamic principle of avoiding israf (waste), Qur'an 7:31 forbids extravagance.

teach.heading: Managing traffic

head: Strategy
How it works
Possible drawback
rows: Pay to drive in central zone
Park outside, use bus or tram
One card for tube, bus and rail

teach.note: Match each strategy to its problem. London Congestion Charge started in 2003 and the ULEZ (ultra-low emission zone) was introduced in central London in 2019 and expanded to all boroughs in 2023; charge levels change so teacher should verify. Ask: who is helped and who is disadvantaged by a charge? (Low-income drivers.)

teach.heading: Model: a 9-mark judgement paragraph

model.problem: One paragraph: To what extent was the regeneration of Stratford successful?
steps: Economic: derelict land became Westfield Stratford City and offices, creating jobs.
Social: East Village added homes, but affordable housing was limited and prices rose.
Environmental: contaminated brownfield land was cleaned and parkland and wetland created.
Counter: some local residents did not get the new jobs or could not afford the homes.
Judgement: largely successful for the area's image and environment, partly successful for local people.
model.answer: A balanced judgement which weighs evidence from three themes and reaches a reasoned verdict.

teach.note: Show how to build a judgement across social, economic and environmental criteria. Pupils highlight evidence, explanation and verdict in three colours.

practice: Describe two features of the Olympic Park regeneration. (2 marks)
Explain why regeneration of Stratford was needed. (3 marks)
independent: Core: Explain how traffic management strategies can reduce congestion in cities. (4 marks)
Extend: Suggest one reason the benefits of the Olympic regeneration may not reach all local people. (3 marks)
Stretch: To what extent was the regeneration of Stratford successful? (9 marks, plus 3 SPaG marks)
exit: Define regeneration.
Name one traffic management strategy and one drawback.
lessons.homework: Design a sustainable neighbourhood: sketch it and label five features with reasons.
lessons.send: SEND: sorting cards for benefits and criticisms. EAL: glossary. Stretch: compare Stratford with Detroit or Manchester's Salford Quays.

lessons.title: A human enquiry and evaluating fieldwork: quality of life along a transect
lessons.bigQuestion: How reliable are our conclusions, and what are the limits of an enquiry?
objectives: Present and analyse human geography data using averages and range
Identify anomalies and suggest explanations
Evaluate method, reliability and the limits of conclusions
successCriteria: All: calculate mean, median and range
Most: describe the pattern and identify an anomaly
Some: evaluate reliability and suggest improvements
lessons.crossCurricular: Mathematics: averages and range; PSHE: wellbeing and community
lessons.smsc: Social: caring for the local environment as a shared trust

keywords.def: a scored assessment of an area's appearance, noise, litter and safety
a line along which data is collected at regular intervals
the sum of values divided by the number of values
the middle value when data is in order
the difference between the highest and lowest values
a value that does not fit the overall pattern

starter: Bismillah. Name two sampling methods.
Define reliability.
What is a transect?

teach.heading: The enquiry
bullets: Question: how does environmental quality change with distance from the centre of a town?
Hypothesis: quality improves with distance from the centre.
Method: environmental quality survey at 6 sites, scored out of 30.
teach.note: Say clearly that the dataset is invented for teaching, to model how real data would look. For online learners real data can be obtained from published town surveys; AQA still requires primary data for at least two enquiries. Link to urban unit: regeneration and quality of life. Ask: what could count as human-physical interaction in this enquiry? (River flooding of low-lying central areas.)

teach.heading: Calculate and present

model.problem: Calculate the mean, median and range of the environmental quality scores.
model.answer: Mean 15.5, median 13.5, range 15.

teach.note: Model the calculation aloud: sum 9 + 12 + 15 + 21 + 24 + 12 = 93, mean 93 / 6 = 15.5. Order data: 9, 12, 12, 15, 21, 24, so median = (12 + 15) / 2 = 13.5. Range = 24 - 9 = 15. The mean is pulled up by the high scores; the median is less affected. Suggest displaying as a bar chart or a radar graph, with sites on the x-axis.

teach.heading: Analyse and find the anomaly

check.q: Which result is an anomaly in the transect data?
check.why: Quality rises with distance until site 6, which drops to 12. The others fit the rising trend. Ignoring the anomaly would misrepresent the data.

teach.note: Use the check. Site 6 is the anomaly, scoring 12 at 5 km. Possible explanations: next to a busy ring road, a retail park or a landfill. Teach pupils never to ignore anomalies: explain and consider repeating. Link to reliability.

teach.heading: Conclusions
bullets: State whether the hypothesis is supported and why.
Give a possible geographical reason for the pattern.

timeline.label: Step 1
timeline.text: Restate the hypothesis

timeline.label: Step 2
timeline.text: Describe the main trend with figures

timeline.label: Step 3
timeline.text: Explain using geographical ideas

timeline.label: Step 4
timeline.text: Mention anomalies and limits

teach.note: Model an example: 'The data mostly supports the hypothesis: quality rose from 9 at 0.5 km to 24 at 4 km. Inner areas have traffic, litter and older housing. However site 6 breaks the trend.' Remind pupils to avoid claims the data cannot support.

teach.heading: Evaluating the enquiry

head: Issue
Effect on reliability
Improvement
rows: Use one scoring guide and two surveyors

teach.note: Prompt pupils: what would improve it? More sites, repeat on different days, more than one surveyor to reduce bias, include areas other than one transect. Distinguish reliability (repeatable) from validity (does it measure what we want). Link to exam: 'evaluate' needs strengths, weaknesses and a judgement.

practice: Calculate the mean score for sites 1 to 5 only. (2 marks)
Suggest why site 6 is an anomaly. (2 marks)
independent: Core: Describe the pattern in the data. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how the enquiry could be made more reliable. (4 marks)
Stretch: Evaluate how far the data supports the hypothesis and the limits of the conclusion. (6 marks)
exit: Which is more affected by an anomaly: mean or median?
Name one way to make an enquiry more reliable.
lessons.homework: Write the evaluation section for a fieldwork enquiry you plan to carry out locally.
