FLAG FOR TEACHER: AQA requires two fieldwork enquiries (one physical, one human, in two contrasting environments, with primary data collected on at least two outside-school occasions) and a signed centre fieldwork statement; the spec pack states secondary data alone does not meet this. An online cohort might meet it through supervised local fieldwork with a parent or tutor using a standard data pack, a partner centre or a residential day; the school must confirm this with AQA before relying on it. This lesson uses secondary data to teach the method only.

lessons.title: Climate change and tropical storms: more, stronger or different?
lessons.bigQuestion: Will a warmer world bring more powerful storms, and to whom?
objectives: Describe how climate change may alter the distribution, frequency and intensity of tropical storms
Explain the links between sea temperature, sea level and storm impacts
Evaluate how certain scientists are about these changes
successCriteria: All: say what may change about tropical storms
Most: explain why warmer seas and higher sea levels matter
Some: evaluate the certainty of predictions
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: energy transfer and the greenhouse effect
lessons.smsc: Moral: responsibility to those most at risk from climate change (khilafah, stewardship)

keywords.def: where something occurs across the world
how often an event happens
how strong an event is, such as wind speed
a rise in sea level caused by low pressure and strong winds
the temperature of the top layer of the ocean

starter: Bismillah. At what sea temperature do tropical storms usually form?
Name three conditions needed for a tropical storm.
Name the main greenhouse gas added by burning fossil fuels.

teach.heading: Three things that could change
bullets: Distribution: where storms form and track.
Frequency: how many storms occur each year.
Intensity: wind speed, rainfall and storm surge.
teach.note: Link the starter to the formation lesson: warm sea water is the fuel. Use the three words to organise the lesson, then ask pupils to predict each. Be careful: scientists are more confident about some changes than others. The prediction is described as 'may', never certain.

teach.heading: Warmer seas: distribution and intensity
bullets: Warmer oceans may allow storms to form further from the equator.
More heat energy may lead to stronger winds and heavier rain.
Some areas may see storms reaching places that rarely had them.
teach.note: Explain that tropical storms need sea surface temperatures of about 27 degrees C or more (approx.). If more ocean exceeds this, the potential area widens slightly. Stronger storms are expected because more energy and water vapour are available. Be honest: evidence that storms are moving poleward is still being researched; use cautious language such as 'may' and 'projected'. Case-study figures are approximate; verify against current sources before teaching.

teach.heading: Frequency and sea level
bullets: Total number of storms may stay similar or fall.
A greater share of storms may be the most intense categories.
Higher sea level makes storm surges reach further inland.
teach.note: Many studies suggest the total number of tropical storms might not rise, while the proportion of strong storms might. Ask why you would still prepare. Sea-level rise adds to storm surge: the same storm floods more land. This links to Haiyan and to low-lying coasts such as Bangladesh. State this as a projection not a fact.

teach.heading: Applying it to the UK
teach.note: UK weather hazards are not tropical storms but climate change is linked to heavier rainfall, hotter summers and rising sea level. Use the July 2022 heatwave from the earlier lesson: 40 degrees C recorded for the first time in the UK (verify). A warmer atmosphere holds more water vapour, so heavy rainfall events may become more frequent. Keep to statements pupils can justify.

head: Hazard
Possible change
rows: Stronger winds, heavier rain, higher surge

teach.heading: How sure are we?
teach.note: Model the evaluation: describe the change, give the cause, then state the uncertainty. Use 'it is likely that', 'some studies suggest'. A 6-mark question wants balanced discussion and a judgement.

model.problem: Discuss how climate change may alter tropical storms. (4 marks)
steps: Intensity: warmer sea surface gives more energy so winds and rainfall may increase
Distribution: warm water may extend further from the equator so storms may affect new areas
Frequency: total numbers may not rise, though the proportion of intense storms may
Sea level: higher seas increase storm surge and flooding
model.answer: Three or four linked points showing cause and effect, with careful wording

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer C. A confuses frequency with intensity. B overstates certainty. D reverses cause and effect.

check.q: Which statement is the most accurate about climate change and tropical storms?
options: Storms will definitely form every month of the year
More heat energy may make the strongest storms more intense
Sea level rise reduces storm surge
check.why: Warmer seas give more energy so intense storms may become stronger; the evidence for frequency and distribution is less certain and sea-level rise increases surges.

practice: Complete: a warmer ocean means ... energy for storms, so wind speeds may ...
Explain why a rise in sea level makes a storm surge more dangerous.
independent: Core: Describe two ways climate change may affect tropical storms. (4 marks)
Extend: Explain how climate change may alter the distribution, frequency and intensity of tropical storms. (6 marks)
Stretch: 'Scientists are certain climate change will make tropical storms worse.' How far do you agree? (6 marks)
exit: Name the three things that may change.
Return to the big question: who is most at risk?
lessons.homework: Write a 100-word briefing for a coastal community on how climate change may affect storm risk.
lessons.send: SEND: sentence starters for cause and effect. EAL: key terms with pictures. Stretch: compare projections for the Atlantic and Pacific.

lessons.unit: Unit 3.1.2.3: Hot deserts (3.1.2) - option, hot deserts or cold environments
lessons.title: Why does fragile land turn to desert? Weighing the causes of desertification
lessons.bigQuestion: Which cause of desertification is hardest to stop, and why?
objectives: State and explain each cause: climate change, population growth, fuelwood removal, overgrazing, over-cultivation, soil erosion
Show how the causes link together
Judge which causes are most important in a given place
successCriteria: All: list the causes of desertification
Most: explain how each cause damages land
Some: link causes and justify which matters most
lessons.crossCurricular: Science: soil structure and nutrients
lessons.smsc: Moral: stewardship (khilafah) of land and fairness to local people

keywords.def: land degradation in dry areas so it becomes desert-like
trees and branches cut for cooking and heating
too many animals on land strip the plants
growing crops too often so the soil loses nutrients
removal of topsoil by wind or water

starter: Bismillah. Define desertification.
Name one place at risk, such as the Sahel.
What is the rainfall total of a hot desert, approximately?

teach.heading: From pressure to degradation
bullets: Dry-land ecosystems are fragile: plants and soil are thin.
Cause and effect chains show how.
teach.note: Revisit the first lesson on desertification, but go further: the exam question wants explanation, not lists. Introduce the six causes on the board. Say: every cause leads to the same outcome, bare soil. Ask pupils to predict what happens next once the cover is lost.

teach.heading: Climate change and population growth
bullets: Higher temperatures and less rainfall can cause drought.
More people need more food, water and fuel.
Pressure on a limited land area rises.
teach.note: Climate change: parts of the Sahel and Central Asia may become drier; plants die; soil dries and blows away. Population growth: more people, more livestock, more farms on the same land. Link them: population growth is a driver of the other human causes. Avoid saying all drylands are expanding; the pattern varies and evidence is debated.

teach.heading: Fuelwood, overgrazing and over-cultivation
bullets: Fuelwood removal: trees cut for cooking and heating.
Overgrazing: too many animals strip plants and compact soil.
Over-cultivation: no rest for the soil so nutrients run out.
teach.note: Explain each as a chain. Fuelwood removal: families with no other fuel cut trees; roots no longer hold soil. Overgrazing: animals eat and trample plants faster than they regrow. Over-cultivation: repeated crops without fallow or fertiliser remove nutrients, plants grow poorly and soil is exposed. Ask why people do these things (poverty, no alternative); this is empathy, not blame.

teach.heading: Soil erosion: the result and the cause
teach.note: Draw the cycle; show it as a feedback loop. Wind and heavy rain remove the topsoil that holds nutrients and water. Lower fertility means fewer plants and more bare soil, so more erosion. Soil erosion both results from the other causes and worsens the problem. Pupils should write the cycle in their own words.
cycle: Land less fertile, less water stored

teach.heading: Link the causes and judge
teach.note: Model the 6-mark thinking: explain, link, judge. Then ask pupils to decide which cause is hardest to solve (population growth and poverty-driven fuelwood use are deep-rooted; climate change is global).

model.problem: Explain how overgrazing and population growth contribute to desertification. (4 marks)
steps: Population growth means more people and livestock need food and land
More livestock means plants are eaten faster than they regrow
Roots no longer bind soil so wind and rain erode topsoil
The land becomes infertile and desert-like
model.answer: Linked chain from population growth to overgrazing to soil erosion

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer A. B is a result, not a cause. C mixes protection with cause. D is a management strategy.

check.q: Which is a cause of desertification linked to cooking and heating?
check.why: Cutting trees for fuel leaves soil exposed to erosion. The others are ways to reduce desertification.

practice: Put these causes in a chain: population growth, overgrazing, bare soil, soil erosion.
Why is population growth hard to separate from the other causes?
independent: Core: Name four causes of desertification. (4 marks)
Extend: Explain how over-cultivation and fuelwood removal cause desertification. (6 marks)
Stretch: 'Human activity is the main cause of desertification.' How far do you agree? (6 marks)
exit: Define over-cultivation.
Return to the big question: which cause is hardest to stop and why?
lessons.homework: Create a poster showing how the six causes link to one another.
lessons.send: SEND: chain cards. EAL: sentence stems with 'so', 'which leads to'. Stretch: research a place where desertification is being reversed.

lessons.unit: Unit 3.1.3.1: UK physical landscapes (3.1.3 Physical landscapes in the UK)
lessons.title: Using the UK overview as a base: why do landscapes differ across Britain?
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a map of the UK help predict what a landscape looks like?
objectives: Use the overview of the UK's uplands, lowlands, rivers and rock types to predict landscape features
Link rock type, past glaciation and processes to landscapes
Choose a landscape study and apply the overview to it
successCriteria: All: locate uplands and lowlands
Most: link rock type to relief
Some: use the overview to explain a chosen landscape
lessons.crossCurricular: Geology and history: the Ice Age legacy
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: reflecting on Allah's variety in creation (landscape and people)

keywords.def: high land with steeper slopes and often harder rock
low-lying land with gentle slopes
rock that erodes slowly
the effect of ice sheets and glaciers on land
the height and shape of land

starter: Bismillah. Name two uplands in the UK.
Name one major UK river.
What is erosion?

teach.heading: Uplands and lowlands
bullets: Uplands are mainly in the north and west.
Lowlands are mainly in the south and east.
Rock type and glaciation help explain this.
teach.note: Show a relief map of the UK. Ask pupils to find the Scottish Highlands, Lake District, Pennines, Snowdonia and south-west uplands. The overview from lesson 23 is the base. The point now is application: from the map, what can we predict?

teach.heading: Hard rock, soft rock
bullets: North and west: older, harder rocks such as granite.
South and east: younger, softer rocks such as clay.
Hard rocks erode slowly and form higher land.
teach.note: Keep the generalisation but flag exceptions: chalk is relatively resistant but forms lowland hills (the Downs and Wolds). Hard rock tends to form upland; soft rock forms lowland and eroded coasts. Link to coastal and river landscapes: soft rock coasts such as Holderness erode quickly.

left.title: North and west
points: Harder rocks such as granite and slate
Heavier rainfall, ice sheets once covered

right.title: South and east
points: Softer rocks such as clay and sand
Less rainfall, more erosion by sea

teach.heading: Ice, rivers and coasts
bullets: Glaciers carved the upland valleys and left lakes.
Rivers flow from uplands toward the sea.
Coasts differ with rock type and wave energy.
teach.note: Link to lessons on the Lake District glaciation and River Tees. Rivers rise in the uplands (Tees in the Pennines) and flow east or south toward lower land. The overview becomes a toolkit: relief shows where rivers are steep, rock type shows which coast erodes fastest, past ice shows where U-shaped valleys occur.

teach.heading: Applying the overview
teach.note: Worked example: pupils predict for a named place, then check. Keep it as a model: place, rock, relief, process, landform. Use it to introduce the chosen landscape studies (coast, river, glacial).

model.problem: Use the UK overview to predict the coastline and landscape of Holderness (east Yorkshire).
steps: Location: east coast, lowland, in the south and east of the UK
Rock: soft boulder clay left by ice
Processes: waves erode easily so cliffs retreat quickly
Landforms: low cliffs, beaches, and a spit
model.answer: A fast-eroding soft-rock coast with beaches and a spit

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. A is an upland feature. C is the opposite. D mixes climate and rock.

check.q: Which landscape would you predict for a coast of soft clay on the east of England?
options: Steep granite cliffs with few beaches
check.why: Soft rock is easily eroded by waves, so the cliffs retreat quickly. Granite and corries belong to resistant, glaciated uplands.

practice: On a blank map, shade uplands and label the River Severn, Thames and Tyne.
Explain why chalk is an exception to the hard/soft rule.
independent: Core: Describe the pattern of uplands and lowlands in the UK. (3 marks)
Extend: Explain how rock type affects the UK landscape. (4 marks)
Stretch: Use the overview to predict and explain landscape features in the Lake District. (6 marks)
exit: Name two upland areas and one lowland area.
Return to the big question: what can a map predict?
lessons.homework: Choose a UK landscape and write a prediction paragraph using the map and the idea of rock type, relief and ice.
lessons.send: SEND: annotated relief maps. EAL: key words with pictures. Stretch: use a geology map to test the predictions.

lessons.title: Fieldwork requirements: two environments, two visits, physical and human
lessons.bigQuestion: What must a complete fieldwork course include, and how does it link into Paper 3?
objectives: State the requirements: two enquiries in two contrasting environments with at least two outside-school visits
Explain the need to cover physical and human geography and to show their interaction
Plan how your school's enquiries meet the requirements
successCriteria: All: state the requirements
Most: give examples of contrasting environments
Some: explain how physical and human geography can interact
lessons.crossCurricular: PSHE: working safely and collaboratively outdoors
lessons.smsc: Social: respecting local people and the environment while collecting data

keywords.def: a structured investigation answering a question
two different settings, such as a coast and a city
how physical and human geography affect each other
data you collect yourself
data collected by others

starter: Bismillah. List the six stages of an enquiry.
What is a hypothesis?
Give one primary data method.

teach.heading: What the course requires
bullets: At least two visits outside school.
teach.note: Be accurate: the specification requires two enquiries, each in a contrasting environment, using primary data, and at least two outside-school visits. Physical and human geography must both be covered, and at least one enquiry must show interaction. Check the school's own plan and dates; this task covers requirements only. Online school: our fieldwork is arranged by tutors and families; check the school's fieldwork plan.

teach.heading: Two contrasting environments
teach.note: Examples: a river or coast (physical) and an urban area (human) are contrasting. Ask pupils: why do we need contrasting settings? To show different geographical processes and methods. It also gives different data types and risks. For our school, one enquiry might be a physical one such as a river and the other a human one in a town.

teach.heading: Physical and human interaction
bullets: Human activity can change physical processes.
One enquiry must show this link.
teach.note: Give examples: a coastal defence scheme that changes erosion (human affects physical); river flooding affecting land use (physical affects human); tourism and footpath erosion. Ask pupils to think of a question that mixes both: 'How do coastal defences affect beach profile and the local tourist economy?'

teach.heading: Planning a compliant course
teach.note: Model completing the audit using a plan: two enquiries, two settings, two visits, both physical and human covered, interaction shown.

model.problem: A school plans enquiry A on river width and depth, and enquiry B on shop types in the same town centre next to the river. Does the plan meet the requirements?
steps: Two enquiries: yes
Contrasting environments: river and town centre can be contrasting
Physical and human both covered: yes, A physical, B human
Interaction: not yet shown; add a question about how the river affects land use or flooding in the town centre
model.answer: Almost. It needs one enquiry that shows interaction

teach.heading: Hinge question
teach.note: Answer B. A is wrong: two settings and two visits. C misses human geography. D: interaction needs showing in at least one.

check.q: Which plan meets the fieldwork requirements?
options: Two enquiries in contrasting settings, physical and human covered, interaction shown
Two physical enquiries in the same place
check.why: The course needs two contrasting settings with physical and human geography and at least one enquiry showing interaction.

practice: List the requirements in your own words.
Suggest a contrasting pair of environments for your area.

Extend: Suggest a fieldwork enquiry that shows the interaction of physical and human geography, and explain why. (4 marks)
Stretch: Plan a pair of enquiries that meet all requirements, giving the question, location and data for each. (6 marks)
exit: Name two contrasting environments.
Return to the big question: what must a course include?
